class-11-notes/biology/floral-diversity/.title: Botany5.1
notes: Classification of the Living World (Botany) — Root to Peak
Diagram:
• Living World (Biology) — Basis: presence of living substance
<ul>
• Protobiota — e.g. Viroids, Viruses, Virions, Prions
• Cytobiota — Basis: cellular organisation
<ul>
• Prokaryotes — e.g. Bacteria, Cyanobacteria
• Mesokaryotes — Members of Dinoflagellates
• Eukaryotes
<ul>
• Plant Kingdom — Acc. to Eichler
<ul>
• Cryptogams
<ul>
• Thallophyta
<ul>
• Algae — e.g. Spirogyra
• Fungi — e.g. Mucor, Yeast, Mushrooms
• Lichens — Algae + Fungi symbiosis
• Bryophyta — e.g. Marchantia, Funaria
• Pteridophyta — e.g. Fern, Selaginella
• Phanerogams
<ul>
• Gymnosperms — e.g. Pinus, Cycas
• Angiosperms
<ul>
• Monocotyledons — e.g. Liliaceae, Poaceae
• Dicotyledons — Acc. to Bentham & Hooker
<ul>
• Polypetalae
• Gamopetalae
• Monochlamydeae
• Animal Kingdom
Exam Notes — All Elements of the Classification
1. Major Classification Systems
Two Kingdom — Linnaeus (1758) — basis: nutrition/motility — Plantae, Animalia.
Three Kingdom — Haeckel (1866) — basis: cell organisation — Protista, Plantae, Animalia.
Four Kingdom — Copeland (1956) — basis: nuclear membrane — Monera, Protista, Plantae, Animalia.
Five Kingdom — R.H. Whittaker (1969) — basis: cell structure, nutrition, body organisation, phylogeny — Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
Six Kingdom — Carl Woese (1977) — basis: rRNA sequencing — Archaebacteria, Eubacteria, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
Three Domain — Carl Woese (1990) — basis: molecular phylogeny — Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya.
Eichler's system (1883) — basis: vascular tissue & seed habit — Cryptogams, Phanerogams.
Bentham & Hooker (1862–83) — basis: floral characters (natural system) — Polypetalae, Gamopetalae, Monochlamydeae, Gymnosperms.
Engler & Prantl (1887–1915) — basis: phylogenetic, simple → complex.
Hutchinson (1926) — basis: phylogenetic — split into Herbaceae and Lignosae lines.
APG (I–IV) — Angiosperm Phylogeny Group — basis: molecular/DNA data — currently the most widely accepted system.
2. Diagnostic Features — Cryptogams
Thallophyta: no vascular tissue, no seed — e.g. Spirogyra, Mucor.
Bryophyta: no vascular tissue, no seed — e.g. Funaria, Marchantia — called "amphibians of the plant kingdom" (need water for fertilisation).
Pteridophyta: true vascular tissue present, reproduces by spores not seeds — e.g. Fern, Equisetum — first vascular plants.
3. Diagnostic Features — Phanerogams
Gymnosperms: naked seed, no fruit, cone-borne — e.g. Pinus, Cycas. Name means "naked seed" (Greek: gymnos = naked, sperma = seed).
Angiosperms: seed enclosed in fruit, flowering plants — e.g. Mango, Wheat.
4. Classes of Algae
Chlorophyceae (green algae, chlorophyll a & b) — e.g. Chlamydomonas, Ulothrix.
Phaeophyceae (brown algae, fucoxanthin) — e.g. Sargassum, Laminaria.
Rhodophyceae (red algae, phycoerythrin) — e.g. Gelidium, Polysiphonia.
Cyanophyceae (blue-green algae, prokaryotic) — e.g. Nostoc, Anabaena.
5. Classes of Fungi
Phycomycetes — aquatic/damp habitat, coenocytic hyphae — e.g. Mucor, Rhizopus.
Ascomycetes — sac fungi, ascospores — e.g. Yeast, Penicillium.
Basidiomycetes — club fungi, basidiospores — e.g. Mushrooms, Rusts, Smuts.
Deuteromycetes — "imperfect fungi", no known sexual stage — e.g. Alternaria, Trichoderma.
6. Classes of Bryophyta
Hepaticopsida (liverworts) — e.g. Marchantia, Riccia.
Anthocerotopsida (hornworts) — e.g. Anthoceros.
Bryopsida (mosses) — e.g. Funaria, Sphagnum.
7. Classes of Pteridophyta
Psilopsida — most primitive, no true roots — e.g. Psilotum.
Lycopsida — club mosses — e.g. Selaginella, Lycopodium.
Sphenopsida — horsetails — e.g. Equisetum.
Pteropsida — true ferns — e.g. Pteris, Dryopteris.
8. Gymnosperm Orders
Cycadales — palm-like stem, motile sperm — e.g. Cycas.
Coniferales — needle-shaped leaves, cones — e.g. Pinus, Cedrus.
Gnetales — vessel elements present (unique among gymnosperms) — e.g. Gnetum, Ephedra.
9. Monocot vs Dicot
Cotyledons: one (monocot) vs two (dicot).
Root system: fibrous/adventitious (monocot) vs tap root (dicot).
Leaf venation: parallel (monocot) vs reticulate (dicot).
Vascular bundles: scattered (monocot) vs ring arrangement (dicot).
Flower parts: trimerous (monocot) vs tetra-/pentamerous (dicot).
Secondary growth: usually absent (monocot) vs usually present (dicot).
Examples: Wheat, Maize, Onion (monocot); Pea, Mustard, Rose (dicot).
10. Bentham & Hooker's Sub-classes of Dicots
Polypetalae — free petals — families: Ranunculaceae, Brassicaceae, Malvaceae, Fabaceae/Papilionaceae, Rosaceae.
Gamopetalae — fused petals — families: Solanaceae, Asteraceae/Compositae, Rubiaceae.
Monochlamydeae — petals absent or single perianth whorl — families: Amaranthaceae, Euphorbiaceae, Moraceae.
Fabaceae is further split by Bentham & Hooker into three sub-families: Papilionoideae, Caesalpinioideae, Mimosoideae — a common one-mark question.
11. Frequently Confused / Testable Points
Viruses are acellular and replicate only inside a host — placed in Protobiota, outside the cellular world.
Mesokaryotes (Dinoflagellates) have a nucleus but lack true nuclear membrane organisation like eukaryotes — an intermediate group.
Cyanobacteria are prokaryotic but historically grouped with algae due to photosynthetic pigments.
Lichens are not a single taxonomic group but a symbiotic association of fungus and alga/cyanobacterium.
Gnetum is a gymnosperm but shows angiosperm-like features (vessels present) — a classic "connecting link" question.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Rutherford's Atomic Model — The Alpha-Particle Scattering Experiment
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: **Experiment:** positively charged helium ions (α-particles) were fired at an ultra-thin gold foil
**Observation:** most α-particles passed straight through, undeflected
**Conclusion:** atoms are mostly empty space, with a tiny, dense, positively charged core called the **nucleus**

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Rutherford's Atomic Model — The Stability Crisis (Flaw)
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: According to classical electromagnetic theory, any accelerating charged particle — such as an electron moving in a circular orbit — must continuously radiate energy
If the electron continuously loses energy, it should spiral inward and eventually collapse into the nucleus
Rutherford's model gave no explanation for why atoms are actually stable and this collapse does not happen — this is the model's central defect

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Postulates
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Postulates of Bohr's atomic model and its application
notes: Niels Bohr resolved Rutherford's stability problem by introducing Planck's Quantum Theory
**Stationary orbits:** electrons revolve only in specific, fixed, non-radiating circular paths
**Energy quantization:** energy is only emitted or absorbed when an electron jumps from one orbit to another: ΔE = hν

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Practical Application
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Postulates of Bohr's atomic model and its application
notes: Successfully calculates the exact radius of orbits, the velocity of electrons, and the energy of an electron for hydrogen-like (single-electron) species: H, He⁺, Li²⁺

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Defects
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Defects of Bohr's theory
notes: Failed to predict the spectra of multi-electron atoms, such as Helium or Carbon
Could not explain the splitting of spectral lines under a magnetic field (**Zeeman Effect**) or an electric field (**Stark Effect**)

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Absorption vs Emission
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Postulates of Bohr's atomic model and its application
notes: While an electron stays within a single stationary orbit, it neither gains nor loses energy
**Jumping up** to an outer (higher-energy) track = absorbing energy
**Dropping down** to an inner (lower-energy) track = releasing energy as a flash of light (a photon)

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Quantization of Angular Momentum
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Defects of Bohr's theory
notes: The postulate that formally restricts which orbits are allowed: the electron's angular momentum is quantized in integer multiples of h/2π
**mvr = nh/2π**, where m = electron mass, v = electron velocity, r = orbit radius, n = 1, 2, 3... (the principal/orbit quantum number)

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: The Hydrogen Spectrum — Origin & Spectral Series
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Spectrum of hydrogen atom
notes: When hydrogen gas is excited (e.g. electrically), electrons absorb energy and jump to higher tracks; when they fall back down to lower tracks, they release that exact energy as light of a specific wavelength
Because transitions happen only between specific fixed tracks, the emitted light forms discrete, sharp spectral lines rather than a continuous rainbow

Each spectral series corresponds to electrons landing on one specific base track (n₁): **Lyman** → n₁ = 1 (ultraviolet, invisible); **Balmer** → n₁ = 2 (the only series visible to the human eye, as coloured lines); **Paschen** → n₁ = 3 (infrared); **Brackett** → n₁ = 4 (infrared); **Pfund** → n₁ = 5 (far-infrared)

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: The Hydrogen Spectrum — Rydberg Equation
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Spectrum of hydrogen atom
notes: 1/λ = R_H·(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), where λ = wavelength of emitted light, R_H = Rydberg constant, n₁ = lower (final) orbit, n₂ = higher (initial) orbit
The **series limit** (shortest wavelength, highest-energy line in a series) occurs as n₂ → ∞, giving the simplified form 1/λ = R_H/n₁²

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Negative Electronic Energy & the Bohr Mechanical Model Critique
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Postulates of Bohr's atomic model and its application
notes: **Negative electronic energy:** the energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit is taken as negative because the electron is bound to the nucleus; energy must be supplied to remove it. The most negative energy corresponds to the most stable (lowest) orbit, n = 1.

**Bohr mechanical model critique:** Bohr treated the electron as a tiny planet moving in a definite circular orbit, a purely mechanical picture. It could not explain why only certain orbits were allowed, nor why the electron did not radiate while moving in a stationary orbit.

**Quantum mechanical shift:** the mechanical orbit picture was replaced by a probabilistic, wave-based description in which the electron's position is described by a wave function rather than a fixed path.

**Schrödinger (1926):** Erwin Schrödinger introduced a wave equation whose solutions (wave functions, ψ) describe the electron's behaviour in three dimensions, giving rise to the modern orbital concept.
**Matter wave introduction:** the idea that particles such as electrons also behave as waves (de Broglie) laid the foundation for the wave-mechanical model.
**Einstein relation:** the equivalence of mass and energy, E = mc², connects the particle and wave descriptions of matter.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: de Broglie Matter Waves & the Einstein–Planck Synthesis
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Elementary idea of quantum mechanical model: de Broglie's wave equation
notes: **Einstein–Planck synthesis:** combining Einstein's mass–energy equivalence E = mc² with Planck's quantum relation E = hν gives mc² = hν, linking a particle's mass to a wave frequency.
**de Broglie wavelength:** since ν = c/λ, the relation becomes mc = h/λ, so the wavelength of a moving particle is λ = h/(mv) = h/p, where p = mv is the momentum.
**Inverse mass dependence:** λ ∝ 1/m — heavier objects have extremely short wavelengths, which is why macroscopic objects show no observable wave behaviour.
**Macro-object wave negligibility:** for everyday objects the de Broglie wavelength is far smaller than any measurable scale, so wave effects are undetectable and classical mechanics applies.

**Bohr quantization deduced via waves:** if an electron is a standing wave, only orbits whose circumference is an integer multiple of the wavelength (2πr = nλ) are stable — this naturally reproduces Bohr's quantization of angular momentum.

**Heisenberg (1927) introduction:** the wave picture of the electron led Heisenberg to the uncertainty principle, which states that position and momentum cannot both be known precisely at the same time.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle (1927)
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle and concept of probability
notes: **Statement:** it is impossible to determine simultaneously and with unlimited precision both the exact position (x) and the exact momentum (p) of a sub-atomic particle such as an electron.
**Mathematical form:** Δx · Δp ≥ h / 4π, where Δx is the uncertainty in position, Δp is the uncertainty in momentum and h = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s is Planck's constant.
**Momentum form:** since Δp = m · Δv, the principle can be written as Δx · Δv ≥ h / (4πm) — for a heavy particle (large m) the product of uncertainties is tiny, so classical certainty is recovered.

**Wavelength measurement intrusion paradox:** observing an electron requires hitting it with photons; a shorter-wavelength photon gives better position information but delivers a larger kick that disturbs the electron's momentum, and vice versa — the act of measurement inevitably perturbs the system.
**Certainty / uncertainty complementarity:** precise knowledge of position destroys knowledge of momentum; the two are complementary and cannot be measured sharply at the same time.
**Probability space concept:** because the electron cannot be pinned to a definite point, its location is described by a probability distribution rather than a fixed path.

**Bohr definite-orbit fallacy:** a precise orbit would require exactly known position and momentum simultaneously, which the uncertainty principle forbids — so Bohr's definite circular orbits are physically impossible.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Schrödinger's Wave Equation & the Orbit→Orbital Shift
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Elementary idea of quantum mechanical model: de Broglie's wave equation
notes: **3D wave equation (1926):** Schrödinger extended de Broglie's idea to three dimensions. For a particle of mass m moving with total energy E and potential energy V, the wave function ψ satisfies (∂²ψ/∂x²) + (∂²ψ/∂y²) + (∂²ψ/∂z²) + (8π²m/h²)(E − V)ψ = 0.

**Wave function interpretation:** ψ itself has no direct physical meaning, but ψ² gives the probability of finding the electron in a small volume around a point — the electron cloud picture replaces the fixed orbit.

**Orbit → orbital paradigm shift:** an orbit is a definite circular path (Bohr), while an orbital is a three-dimensional region of space where the probability of finding the electron is high (usually taken as ~90–95%).

**Quantum numbers emerge naturally:** solving the equation for the hydrogen atom yields three integer quantum numbers (n, l, m) that characterise each allowed orbital, with a fourth (s) added later for spin.
**Subshell subdivision (s, p, d, f):** orbitals of the same principal shell are grouped into subshells labelled s, p, d and f, which differ in shape, energy and orientation.
**Spherical vs directional geometry:** s-orbitals are spherical, while p-orbitals are dumb-bell shaped and directional along the x, y and z axes; d and f orbitals have more complex shapes.
**Electron cloud mapping:** plotting ψ² in three dimensions gives the spatial probability maps (clouds) that replace Bohr's planar circular orbits.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Bohr–Bury Scheme (1921) — Subshell & Shell Capacity Rules
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Defects of Bohr's theory
notes: **Bohr–Bury scheme (1921):** a set of rules for filling electrons into shells and subshells; electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels first (aufbau principle), so the order of filling runs 1s → 2s → 2p → 3s → 3p → 4s → 3d → 4p → 5s → 4d → 5p → 6s → 4f → 5d → 6p → 7s → 5f → 6d → 7p.
**Maximum shell capacity:** the maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n² — K: 2, L: 8, M: 18, N: 32.
**Subshell electron capacity:** s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10, f holds 14 electrons.
**Spatial configurations:** each subshell contains a fixed set of orbitals — s: 1, p: 3, d: 5, f: 7 — so a shell of principal quantum number n contains a total of n² orbitals.
**Valence shell limit:** the outermost (valence) shell can hold at most 8 electrons.
**Penultimate shell limit:** the second-outermost (penultimate) shell can hold at most 18 electrons; the third-outermost (antepenultimate) shell at most 32.
**Concentric capacity rings:** the electrons are distributed in concentric shells (K, L, M, N, …) around the nucleus, each ring accommodating its characteristic maximum.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Orbit vs Orbital — 10-Point Delta Table & the s-Orbital
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only
notes: **Orbit vs orbital (10-point delta):** (1) an orbit is a definite circular path; an orbital is a region of high probability. (2) Orbits are planar; orbitals are three-dimensional. (3) Orbits come from Bohr's model; orbitals from quantum mechanics. (4) An orbit has a fixed radius; an orbital has no sharp boundary. (5) Orbits are described by one quantum number (n); orbitals by three (n, l, m). (6) Orbits imply exact position and momentum; orbitals obey the uncertainty principle. (7) Orbits can hold at most 2n² electrons; orbitals hold at most 2 electrons. (8) Orbits are circular; orbitals have varied shapes (spherical, dumb-bell, etc.). (9) Orbits are not observable; orbitals are mapped by probability density ψ². (10) Orbits were abandoned; orbitals are the accepted modern description.

**Electronic arrays:** the electron configurations of representative atoms follow the Bohr–Bury order — N (Z=7): 1s² 2s² 2p³; O (Z=8): 1s² 2s² 2p⁴; Ne (Z=10): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶; Mg (Z=12): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s²; Cl (Z=17): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵.

**s-orbital sharp metrics:** the s-orbital is spherical, non-directional, has no nodal plane, and its probability density is highest at the nucleus; it is the only orbital with a non-zero value at the nucleus.
**Opposite spins cancellation:** two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins (+½ and −½); their magnetic moments cancel, so a fully paired orbital contributes no net magnetism.
**Energy trend:** for a given principal shell the s-subshell lies lowest in energy: 1s < 2s < 3s < 4s < …

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: p-Orbital Geometry & the Four Quantum Numbers
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Quantum numbers
notes: **p-orbital dumb-bell axes:** each p-orbital is dumb-bell (figure-of-eight) shaped with two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus, oriented along one of the three cartesian axes — pₓ, pᵧ and p_z — which are mutually perpendicular.
**Nodal plane zero points:** every p-orbital has a nodal plane through the nucleus where the probability of finding the electron is zero; for pₓ the nodal plane is the yz-plane, and so on.
**Degenerate energy states:** in a given shell all three p-orbitals have the same energy (they are degenerate); in the absence of a magnetic field they are indistinguishable energetically.

**Complex d/f shapes:** d-orbitals (l = 2) mostly have four-lobed cloverleaf shapes (with one two-lobed d_z² orbital plus a torus), while f-orbitals (l = 3) have even more complex multi-lobed geometries.

**Four quantum numbers categorical taxonomy:** every electron is uniquely specified by (1) the principal quantum number n (main energy level/shell), (2) the azimuthal quantum number l (subshell/shape), (3) the magnetic quantum number m (orbital orientation), and (4) the spin quantum number s (+½ or −½, direction of spin).
**Subshell maximum capacities:** s holds 2 electrons, p holds 6, d holds 10, f holds 14.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Quantum Number Origins — Principal, Azimuthal & Subshell Metrics
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Quantum numbers
notes: **Schrödinger/Spin origins breakdown:** the principal (n), azimuthal (l) and magnetic (m) quantum numbers arise naturally as the three quantum conditions of Schrödinger's wave equation; the spin quantum number (s) was added later from the Stern–Gerlach and Goudsmit–Uhlenbeck experiments.
**Principal quantum number (n):** fixes the main energy level and size of the orbital (shell). n = 1, 2, 3, …; larger n means a larger, higher-energy orbital farther from the nucleus.

**Sommerfeld hyperfine line expansions:** Arnold Sommerfeld introduced the azimuthal (orbital) quantum number l to explain the hyperfine splitting of spectral lines observed under high resolution, which Bohr's model could not explain.
**Subsidiary (azimuthal) quantum number (l):** fixes the subshell and shape of the orbital; l takes integer values 0 to n − 1 and is labelled by letters — s: 0, p: 1, d: 2, f: 3.
**Subshell orbital count:** each subshell contains 2l + 1 orbitals — for s (l=0): 1, p (l=1): 3, d (l=2): 5, f (l=3): 7.
**Subshell electron count:** each subshell holds a maximum of 2(2l + 1) electrons — for s: 2, p: 6, d: 10, f: 14.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Orbital Designation Matrix — Magnetic & Spin Quantum Numbers
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Quantum numbers
notes: **Tabular orbital designation matrix:** the complete set of orbitals for a given shell is catalogued by combining n, l and m. For n = 2: l = 0 gives the single 2s orbital (m = 0); l = 1 gives the three 2p orbitals (m = +1, 0, −1), designated 2pₓ, 2pᵧ, 2p_z.
**Magnetic quantum number (m):** fixes the orientation of the orbital in space relative to an applied magnetic field; m takes 2l + 1 integer values from −l to +l.
**m value sets by subshell:** for l = 0: m = 0 (1 orbital); l = 1: m = +1, 0, −1 (3 orbitals); l = 2: m = +2, +1, 0, −1, −2 (5 orbitals); l = 3: m = +3, +2, +1, 0, −1, −2, −3 (7 orbitals).
**Total orbitals in a shell:** a shell of principal quantum number n contains exactly n² orbitals, combining all subshells of that shell.

**Landé–Zeeman magnetic orientations:** in an external magnetic field, the degenerate orbitals of a subshell split into distinct energy levels (Zeeman effect), each orbital having a different spatial orientation — one line splits into 2l + 1 components.
**Goudsmit–Uhlenbeck electron axial rotation:** Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck proposed that the electron itself spins about its own axis, producing an intrinsic angular momentum and a tiny magnetic dipole.
**Clockwise vs anticlockwise spins:** the electron's spin can be clockwise or anticlockwise, giving two spin states; the spin quantum number s takes only two values: +½ and −½.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Electron Spin Notation (↑ ↓) & Shell Mapping Matrices
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only
notes: **Arrowhead vector notation:** electrons are drawn as arrowheads — an upward arrow (↑) represents spin +½ (clockwise) and a downward arrow (↓) represents spin −½ (anticlockwise); each box (orbital) can hold at most two arrows of opposite direction.

**Net zero paired magnetic field cancellation:** when an orbital contains two electrons with opposite spins, their magnetic moments are equal and opposite, so the net magnetic field of the pair is zero — the atom as a whole becomes diamagnetic for that pair.

**K shell complete mapping matrix:** the K shell (n = 1) contains only the single 1s orbital; it is filled as 1s¹ (one ↑) for hydrogen and 1s² (↑↓) for helium, where the pair is fully spin-compensated.

**L shell complete mapping matrix:** the L shell (n = 2) contains the 2s orbital plus three 2p orbitals (2pₓ, 2pᵧ, 2p_z). Filling follows Hund's rule — electrons first occupy each orbital singly with parallel spins before pairing: e.g. oxygen (1s² 2s² 2p⁴) shows one paired 2p box (↑↓) and two half-filled boxes (↑, ↑).

**Arrow direction convention:** in electron configuration notation the order of filling is drawn left-to-right across the orbitals of the subshell, and the last electron added determines the arrow direction for half-filled orbitals.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: The Atom & Dalton's Atomic Theory
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: **The composition of matter** was studied in the 18th century by different scientists.

**Atom definition:** all matter is made of millions of tiny particles called atoms. The word 'atom' comes from the Greek (a = absence, tomos = cut), meaning indivisible or indestructible — atoms are the smallest units of matter.
**Dalton's atomic theory (1808):** the concept of the atom was first put forward by the English chemist John Dalton, and his theory laid the foundation of modern atomic theory.
**Discovery of subatomic particles:** towards the end of the 19th century it became known that the atom consists of still smaller particles such as electrons, protons and neutrons.
**Further subatomic particles:** subsequent studies led to the discovery of meson, quark, gluon, neutrino, and antiparticles like positron, antiproton, antineutron etc.

**Fundamental particles:** the small particles present in an atom are called subatomic particles; more than 30 have been discovered. Electron, proton and neutron are the principal subatomic particles, generally referred to as fundamental particles.
Example subatomic particles: electrons, protons, neutrons, a positron (e⁺), meson, neutrino (π±), quark.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: The Electron — Discovery & Properties of Cathode Rays
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only
notes: **Electron definition:** an electron is a negatively charged subatomic particle denoted with the symbol e⁻.
**Discovery (1897):** the electron was first discovered by Joseph John Thomson as a result of a discharge tube experiment.

**Discharge tube experiment:** Thomson filled gas in a specially designed glass tube provided with metal electrodes and passed high voltage electricity at low pressure (10,000 Volts at 10⁻² mmHg) through the tube.
**Cathode rays:** as a result, some rays started to flow from the cathode towards the anode, which are called cathode rays.
**Naming:** the term electron was given by George Johnstone Stoney (in 1891).

**Properties of cathode rays:** (a) they cast a shadow of an object on their way; (b) they travel in a straight line; (c) they are deflected towards the anode of the applied electric field, indicating they carry a negative charge; (d) they produce a heating effect when struck to a thin metal coil; (e) they can penetrate a thin sheet of metals; (f) they cause fluorescence on a zinc sulphide screen; (g) they ionize the gas through which they pass.
**Conclusion:** the observation of the above properties led to the conclusion that cathode rays carry a negative charge with a certain mass.
**Naming as electrons:** J.J. Thomson named cathode rays as electrons, symbolized with e⁻ or as a beta particle.
**Charge and mass:** the charge on an electron is -1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs and the mass is 9.1 × 10⁻²⁸ g, which is equal to 1/1837th of the mass of a hydrogen atom.
**e/m determination:** J.J. Thomson determined the e/m (specific charge) value of the electron and Millikan determined the charge of the electron.
**e/m order:** the increasing order of the value of e/m is neutron < alpha-ray < proton < electron.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: The Proton — Discovery & Properties of Anode Rays
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only
notes: **Proton definition:** a proton is a positively charged subatomic particle denoted with the symbol p⁺.

**Context of discovery:** it was discovered after the discovery of electrons, with the assumption that positive particles must also exist alongside negative particles since an atom is electrically neutral.
**Discovery (1886):** the proton was discovered by Eugen Goldstein by a discharge tube experiment like that for electrons.
**Experiment:** he passed high voltage electricity through a discharge tube filled with hydrogen gas and provided with a perforated metal cathode.
**Chemical equation:** H → H⁺ + e⁻ (proton formation).
**Low pressure:** the discharge was carried out at low pressure.
**Canal rays:** he observed rays travelling opposite to the cathode rays; these were deflected towards the cathode of the applied field and thus called anode rays, positive rays, or canal rays.

**Properties of anode rays:** (a) they cast a shadow of the objects in their path; (b) they travel in a straight line; (c) they are deflected towards the cathode of the applied electric or magnetic field; (d) they cause a heating effect on metal coils; (e) they rotate a small paddle wheel placed on their path.
**Conclusion:** these properties led to the conclusion that anode rays carry a positive charge and possess a certain mass.
**Naming:** these rays were named protons by Goldstein and symbolized with p⁺.
**Charge:** the proton possesses +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulomb of electric charge, equal but opposite in sign to that of an electron.
**Mass:** a proton is much heavier than an electron; its mass is 1.672 × 10⁻²⁴ g, equal to the mass of the hydrogen atom.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: The Neutron — Discovery & Fundamental Particle Characteristics
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only
notes: **Context of discovery:** the discovery of electrons and protons was followed by neutrons; the presence of a third type of sub-atomic particle is justified by the fact that atomic mass is not equal to the total mass of the protons present in an atom — it is much higher, as the mass of the electron is negligible.
**Discovery (1932):** this problem was solved by Sir James Chadwick by discovering the presence of neutral particles in an atom.
**Experiment:** he bombarded α-particles on a thin sheet of Beryllium and observed the emission of highly penetrating particles which were neutral.
**Naming:** Chadwick named the neutral particles neutrons.
**Mass:** neutrons possess a mass of 1.675 × 10⁻²⁴ g, which is slightly greater than that of protons.
**Nuclear reaction:** the nuclear reaction used to produce neutrons between α-ray and Beryllium is: ₂He⁴ + ₄Be⁹ → ₆C¹² + ₀n¹ (neutron).

**Fundamental particle summary:** atoms possess mainly three fundamental sub-atomic particles — electrons, protons, and neutrons. The protons and neutrons are present in the nucleus of an atom and are called nucleons; the electrons revolve around the nucleus in different orbits or shells.

**Characteristics table:** Electron (e⁻): mass 9.1 × 10⁻²⁸ g (0.00055 amu), charge -1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (-4.803 × 10⁻¹⁰ esu), discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897. Proton (p⁺): mass 1.672 × 10⁻²⁴ g (1.00732 amu), charge +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (+4.803 × 10⁻¹⁰ esu), discovered by E. Goldstein in 1886. Neutron (n⁰): mass 1.675 × 10⁻²⁴ g (1.00871 amu), charge 0, discovered by James Chadwick in 1932.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Atomic Number (Z)
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: **Definition:** the number of unit positive charges carried by the nucleus of a neutral atom is known as the atomic number; in other words, the number of protons present in the nucleus of an atom is called the atomic number.

**Neutrality:** an atom is neutral due to the presence of an equal number of positive charges of protons and negative charges of electrons, so the atomic number can be considered as the number of electrons present in a neutral atom.
**Symbol:** the atomic number is generally denoted with the letter Z.
**Origin:** the concept of atomic number was first given by the scientist Moseley in 1913; Moseley formulated the modern periodic table based on increasing atomic numbers.
**Formulas:** Atomic number (Z) = number of protons (p⁺); Number of protons (p⁺) = number of electrons (e⁻) in a neutral atom; Z = p⁺ = e⁻.

**Example:** the atomic number of magnesium is 12, indicating there are 12 protons and 12 electrons in the atom. But the magnesium ion (Mg²⁺) possesses 12 protons and 10 electrons, and its atomic number is 12 and not 10.
**Notation:** in general, the atomic number of an element is written on the left side of the symbol of the element as a subscript.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Mass Number (A) & Isotopes
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only
notes: **Mass number:** the sum of masses of sub-atomic particles contained in an atom is responsible for the mass of that atom. Since the mass of electrons is negligible, the mass of an atom is the sum of the masses of protons and neutrons present in the nucleus; the mass of an atom is concentrated on the nucleus.
**Whole number:** a mass number is a whole number since the number of protons and neutrons are whole numbers; it is generally denoted with the letter A.

**Notation:** the mass number is written as a superscript to the symbol of the element; for an atom (X) whose atomic number is Z and mass number is A, the symbol is written with Z as a subscript and A as a superscript.
**Formulas:** Mass number (A) = atomic number (Z) + number of neutrons (N); A = Z + N; A = p⁺ + n⁰; Mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons.
**Example:** ₁₂Mg²⁴ means the mass number of Mg is 24 amu, i.e., 12 protons and 12 neutrons.

**Isotopes definition:** in 1919, F.W. Aston found that certain elements consist of two or more types of atoms with the same atomic number but different mass numbers, which are called isotopes. The word isotope (coined by Soddy in 1913) comes from two Latin words, isos = the same and topos = position/place.

**Isotope properties:** isotopes are different atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different atomic masses; they possess the same position in the modern periodic table, have the same number of protons and electrons but a different number of neutrons, and possess identical chemical properties (due to same atomic number) but different physical properties (due to different mass numbers).

**Abundance:** around 1000 isotopes have been identified, of which nearly 300 are stable and occur in nature; the stability and natural abundance of isotopes differ. Chlorine has two isotopes, whereas krypton has nearly 20 isotopes. Most abundant isotopes occur from 90-99% with respect to other isotopes, but Cl-35 occurs 75% compared to Cl-37 (25%) in nature.

**Hydrogen isotopes:** hydrogen exists in three isotopic forms — protium (₁H¹), deuterium (₁H²), and tritium (₁H³), denoted with symbols H, D, and T respectively. Out of these, tritium is radioactive. Protium has no neutron, deuterium has one, and tritium has two. Natural abundance: protium 99.98%, deuterium about 0.015%, tritium only 10⁻¹⁵ %.

**Examples:** carbon isotopes ₆C¹², ₆C¹³, ₆C¹⁴ (most abundant ₆C¹²); nitrogen ₇N¹⁴, ₇N¹⁵ (₇N¹⁴); oxygen ₈O¹⁶, ₈O¹⁷, ₈O¹⁸ (₈O¹⁶); neon ₁₀Ne²⁰, ₁₀Ne²¹, ₁₀Ne²² (₁₀Ne²⁰); sulphur ₁₆S³², ₁₆S³³, ₁₆S³⁴, ₁₆S³⁶ (₁₆S³²); chlorine ₁₇Cl³⁵, ₁₇Cl³⁷ (₁₇Cl³⁵); uranium ₉₂U²³³, ₉₂U²³⁵, ₉₂U²³⁸ (₉₂U²³⁸).

**Isotopic effect:** the compounds formed by different isotopes possess different physical and chemical properties due to differences in the mass of the isotopes; this difference is called an isotopic effect. e.g. protium and deuterium separately combine with oxygen to give H₂O and D₂O respectively, whose boiling points, melting points, densities, and ionization constants differ to some extent.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Isobars, Isotones & Isodiaphers
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: **Isobars:** several atoms having the same mass number but different atomic numbers are called isobars. The word 'isobar' derives from two Greek words, isos = equal and baros = heavy.

**Isobar properties:** isobars are atoms of different elements having different atomic numbers but the same mass number; they possess entirely different physical and chemical properties. The total number of nucleons (protons + neutrons) remains the same, while the number of protons and electrons differs.

**Isobar examples:** ₁₈Ar⁴⁰, ₁₉K⁴⁰, and ₂₀Ca⁴⁰ are isobars (same mass number 40); also ₆C¹⁴ and ₇N¹⁴ are isobars. Other examples: (i) ₃₂Ge⁷⁶, ₃₄Se⁷⁶; (ii) ₅₂Te¹³⁰, ₅₄Xe¹³⁰, ₅₆Ba¹³⁰; (iii) ₈₂Pb²¹⁴, ₈₃Bi²¹⁴, ₈₄Po²¹⁴; (iv) ₉₂U²³⁹, ₉₃Np²³⁹, ₉₄Pu²³⁹.

**Isotones:** different atoms having different atomic numbers and mass numbers but the same number of neutrons are called isotones. The word 'isotone' derives from Greek, isos = the same and tonos = neutrons.
**Isotone properties:** isotones have different physical and chemical properties since they are entirely different elements; the number of electrons and protons differ in isotones.
**Isotone examples:** ₆C¹⁴, ₇N¹⁵, and ₈O¹⁶ are isotones because each has the same number of neutrons (8).
**Isodiaphers:** several atoms having the same isotopic number or isotopic excess (number of neutrons − number of protons) are called isodiaphers.
**Isodiapher examples:** ₁₉K³⁹ and ₉F¹⁹ are isodiaphers.
**Nuclear composition of isotones:** ₆C¹⁴ (atomic number 6, mass 14, e⁻ 6, p⁺ 6, n⁰ 8); ₇N¹⁵ (atomic number 7, mass 15, e⁻ 7, p⁺ 7, n⁰ 8); ₈O¹⁶ (atomic number 8, mass 16, e⁻ 8, p⁺ 8, n⁰ 8).

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Thomson's Plum Pudding (Watermelon) Model
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: **Context:** before 1898, the specific location of electrons and protons within an atom remained completely unknown.
**Proposal (1898):** J.J. Thomson proposed a simple model conceptually known as the 'watermelon model' (also called the plum pudding model).
**Structure:** Thomson considered the atom to be a solid sphere of uniform positive charge, with negatively charged electrons embedded within this positive sphere like seeds inside a watermelon.
**Fate:** this model failed to explain many subsequent practical and theoretical findings and was soon discarded.

**Alpha particle tool:** around the same period, radioactive elements like radium were found to produce dipositive helium ions with a charge of 2+ and a mass of 4 amu; an alpha particle is denoted He²⁺ or ₂He⁴, formed by the nuclear equation [He − 2e⁻ → He²⁺].

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Rutherford's Atomic Model
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Rutherford's Atomic Model
notes: This page covers the foundational concepts of an alpha particle and early atomic models (Thomson's and Rutherford's models).
1. Alpha Particle (α)
• Definition: A di-positive helium ion (He²⁺).
• Mass & Charge: It has a charge of 2 + and a mass of 4 amu.
• Notation: Represented as ⁴₂He or He²⁺.
2. Thomson's Model of the Atom
• Concept: Often called the watermelon model or plum pudding model.
• Structure: The atom is imagined as a sphere of uniform positive charge, with negatively charged electrons embedded inside like seeds in a watermelon.
• Outcome: Discarded quickly because it could not explain later experimental results, specifically large-angle scattering.
3. Rutherford's α-Particle Scattering Experiment (1911)
• Setup: High-energy alpha particles from a radioactive source (like Radium) were passed through a slit in a lead plate and directed at a very thin gold foil (0.00006 cm thick).
• Detection: A circular, movable zinc sulphide (ZnS) screen flashed tiny spots of light (scintillations) when struck by alpha particles.
Observations & The Fate of Bombarded Particles
• Most particles: Passed straight through the foil without changing direction.
• A few particles: Were slightly deflected from their original path.
• Very few particles: Were heavily deflected or reflected backward.
Conclusion Highlighted on the Page
Millions of shining spots over a large area indicate that the atom is mostly empty space. The tiny region causing heavy deflections represents the small, dense, positively charged nucleus.
📊 Statistical Observations
• ~99% of particles: Passed straight through the gold foil.
• Some particles: Deflected by small angles.
• ~1 in 10,000: Deflected by large angles of 90° or more.
• 1 in 20,000: Bounced directly backward, suffering a 180° deflection.
💡 Conclusions Drawn
• Empty Space: Most of the interior of an atom is hollow or empty because nearly all particles passed straight through.
• Positive Core: A heavy, positively charged center exists because like charges repel, causing the positive α-particles to deflect.
• Tiny Volume: The nucleus is exceptionally small compared to the total size of the atom.
◦ Nucleus radius: 10⁻¹³ cm (1 fermi)
◦ Atom radius: 10⁻⁸ cm
🔬 Observations of α-Particle Scattering
• Straight Penetration: Most α-particles (~99%) passed completely straight through the gold foil.
• Small Deflections: Some α-particles were deflected through small angles.
• Large Deflections: Very few particles (about 1 in 10,000) bounced back at angles larger than 90°.
• Reversal: Approximately 1 in 20,000 particles suffered a maximum deflection of 180°.
💡 Conclusions Drawn
• Hollow Atom: Most space inside the atom is empty because particles passed straight through.
• Positive Core: A heavy, positively charged body exists at the center to repel positive α-particles.
• Tiny Volume: The central core occupies an extremely small volume relative to the entire atom.
• Massive Nucleus: The central core contains almost all the atom's mass, enabling it to reflect heavy particles.
🪐 Postulates of Rutherford's Nuclear Model
• The Nucleus: An atom consists of a tiny, positively charged center called the nucleus (radius ≈ 10⁻¹³ cm).
• Electronic Cloud: Electrons surround the nucleus within a much larger radius (atom radius ≈ 10⁻⁸ cm).
• Size Difference: The overall size of an atom is about 10⁵ (100,000) times larger than its nucleus.
• Electrostatic Attraction: Strong Coulombic electrostatic forces hold the negatively charged electrons and the positively charged nucleus together.
• Electrical Neutrality: The total number of protons inside the nucleus equals the number of electrons outside it, making the atom electrically neutral.

• Planetary Motion: Electrons revolve continuously around the nucleus in circular paths (orbits). The electrostatic pull toward the center is balanced by the outward centrifugal force. Because of this similarity to planets orbiting the sun, it is called the planetary atomic model.
1. The Stability Defect
• Continuous Energy Loss: Accelerated charged particles (like revolving electrons) must continuously radiate energy.
• Spiral Collapse: The electron should spiral inward as it loses energy and crash into the nucleus, making the atom unstable.
2. The Spectrum Defect
• Expected vs. Real: The model predicts a continuous spectrum due to continuous energy loss.
• Line Spectrum: In reality, atoms produce a line spectrum (discrete wavelengths), which this model cannot explain.
3. The Electronic Structure Defect
• Arrangement: The model states that electrons revolve around the nucleus, but it remains completely silent about how they are distributed or arranged in their orbits.
• Energy Levels: It does not explain the specific energies associated with these electronic paths.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Introduction to Chemistry
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Introduction to Chemistry
notes: Chemistry is the branch of science that studies matter, its properties, composition, and changes.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Q: State the observations and conclusions of Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only
notes: **Observation 1:** most α-particles passed straight through the gold foil undeflected → most of the atom's volume is empty space

**Observation 2:** a small fraction were deflected at large angles, and a very small fraction bounced almost straight back → these particles must have encountered something small, dense, and positively charged
**Conclusion:** the atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre, with electrons occupying the mostly empty space around it

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Q: Why does Rutherford's nuclear model fail to explain the stability of an atom?
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Spectrum of hydrogen atom
notes: Maxwell's theory states that any accelerating charge radiates electromagnetic energy
An electron orbiting the nucleus is constantly changing direction, so it is constantly accelerating, and by Maxwell's theory it should continuously lose energy as radiation

Losing energy means the electron's orbital radius should shrink, causing it to spiral inward and collapse into the nucleus within a fraction of a second — but real atoms are stable, which Rutherford's model cannot account for

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Q: How exactly did Bohr's model resolve the stability crisis left unsolved by Rutherford?
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: Bohr proposed that electrons can only exist in specific 'stationary' orbits where they do NOT radiate energy, regardless of their acceleration — this postulate directly overrides the classical prediction that orbiting charges must radiate
Energy changes only happen in discrete jumps between these fixed orbits (ΔE = hν), not continuously, so there's no mechanism for a gradual energy loss and inward spiral

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Q: Bohr's model works well for hydrogen but fails for helium — why does adding one more electron break the model?
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Defects of Bohr's theory
notes: Bohr's postulates and resulting equations were derived by balancing the electrostatic attraction between a single electron and the nucleus against the centripetal force needed for circular motion — a clean two-body problem

With two or more electrons, electron–electron repulsion enters the picture, making it a multi-body problem that Bohr's simple circular-orbit model has no mechanism to account for — this is why it accurately predicts the spectra of H, He⁺, and Li²⁺ (all single-electron species) but not neutral He or heavier atoms

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Q: What do the Zeeman and Stark effects reveal about the limits of Bohr's model?
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Defects of Bohr's theory
notes: **Zeeman Effect:** spectral lines split into multiple closely spaced lines when the atom is placed in a magnetic field
**Stark Effect:** spectral lines split when the atom is placed in an electric field

Bohr's model treats each orbit as having a single fixed energy, so it cannot explain why a magnetic or electric field would split a single spectral line into several — this splitting requires additional quantum numbers (like the magnetic quantum number) that only came with the more advanced quantum mechanical model of the atom

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Q: State the three main observations of Rutherford's gold foil experiment and their corresponding conclusions
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only
notes: **Observation 1:** most α-particles passed straight through the foil undeflected → **Conclusion:** atoms are mostly empty space

**Observation 2:** a small fraction were deflected through small-to-moderate angles → **Conclusion:** there is a concentration of positive charge somewhere in the atom that repels the positively charged α-particles

**Observation 3:** a very small fraction (about 1 in 8000) bounced back at large angles, close to 180° → **Conclusion:** this positive charge, along with almost all of the atom's mass, is concentrated in an extremely small volume — the nucleus

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Q (worked example): Calculate the radius of the electron in the 2nd orbit of a Li²⁺ ion
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Spectrum of hydrogen atom
notes: Bohr radius formula: r_n = (0.529 Å)·n²/Z, where n = orbit number and Z = atomic number
For Li²⁺: Z = 3, n = 2
**Answer: r₂ ≈ 0.705 Å**

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Q (worked example): Calculate the wavelength of the series limit of the Lyman series for hydrogen
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Spectrum of hydrogen atom
notes: The series limit occurs as n₂ → ∞, so 1/λ = R_H(1/n₁² − 0) = R_H/n₁²
For the Lyman series, n₁ = 1: 1/λ = 1.097 × 10⁷ × 1 = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹
**Answer: λ ≈ 91.15 nm** — deep ultraviolet, consistent with the Lyman series being a UV series

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Q: Which hydrogen spectral series falls entirely within the visible region of light, and why is it the only one?
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Spectrum of hydrogen atom
notes: The **Balmer series** (n₁ = 2) is the only series entirely visible to the human eye
Its emitted wavelengths (transitions from n₂ = 3, 4, 5... down to n₁ = 2) happen to fall in the roughly 400–700 nm range that human eyes detect

The Lyman series (n₁ = 1) is higher-energy and shorter-wavelength (ultraviolet), while Paschen, Brackett, and Pfund (n₁ = 3, 4, 5) are lower-energy and longer-wavelength (infrared) — both fall outside the visible window

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Self-Practice Checkpoint — Negative Energy & Bohr Critique (Page 108)
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Defects of Bohr's theory
notes: **Q1. Why is the energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit taken as negative?** Because the electron is bound to the nucleus; energy must be supplied to remove it. The most negative energy corresponds to the most stable (lowest) orbit, n = 1.

**Q2. State two major defects of Bohr's atomic model.** (1) It could not explain why only certain orbits are allowed (quantization was assumed, not derived). (2) It could not explain the spectra of atoms with more than one electron (e.g. helium), nor the fine structure of spectral lines.

**Q3. What is the significance of E = mc² in the development of quantum mechanics?** It links mass and energy, and combined with Planck's E = hν it leads to the de Broglie relation λ = h/(mv), showing that matter has wave-like properties.

**Q4. How did Schrödinger's 1926 work shift the atomic model?** Schrödinger replaced Bohr's definite circular orbits with a wave equation whose solutions (wave functions ψ) describe the electron's behaviour in three dimensions, giving rise to the probabilistic orbital concept.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Self-Practice Checkpoint — Duality & Principle Deflections (Page 111)
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle and concept of probability
notes: **Q1. Distinguish between an orbit and an orbital.** An orbit is a definite circular path of the electron (Bohr model), planar and described by one quantum number n. An orbital is a three-dimensional region of high probability of finding the electron (quantum mechanics), described by three quantum numbers (n, l, m) and obeying the uncertainty principle.

**Q2. What is the physical significance of the wave function ψ and of ψ²?** ψ itself has no direct physical meaning; ψ² gives the probability density of finding the electron in a small volume around a point, which is used to map the electron cloud.

**Q3. Why did the wave-mechanical model replace Bohr's definite orbits?** Because the uncertainty principle forbids knowing position and momentum simultaneously, a definite orbit is impossible; the electron must instead be described by a probability distribution (orbital).

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Self-Practice Checkpoint — Numerical Verifications & Degeneracy Mappings (Page 114)
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: **Q1. How many orbitals are present in the subshell with l = 2? What is its maximum electron capacity?** Number of orbitals = 2l + 1 = 2(2) + 1 = 5. Maximum electron capacity = 2(2l + 1) = 10. So the d subshell has 5 orbitals and holds up to 10 electrons.

**Q2. Write the four quantum numbers that completely describe an electron in the 3p orbital.** Principal n = 3, azimuthal l = 1, magnetic m = −1, 0 or +1 (three possible values), spin s = +½ or −½. Any one of the six possible combinations (3 values of m × 2 spins) describes an electron in 3p.

**Q3. How many degenerate orbitals are there in a p subshell, and why are they called degenerate?** There are three (pₓ, pᵧ, p_z). They have the same energy (they are degenerate) in the absence of an applied magnetic field.

**Q4. For the d subshell, verify the degeneracy mapping.** With l = 2, m takes the values +2, +1, 0, −1, −2, giving 2l + 1 = 5 degenerate orbitals; each holds 2 electrons, so the d subshell accommodates 10 electrons in total.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Q (worked examples): de Broglie Wavelength & Uncertainty Principle
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle and concept of probability
notes: **Q1. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving with a velocity of 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s.** Using λ = h/(mv) with h = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg and v = 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s: λ = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 6.6 × 10⁶) = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / 6.006 × 10⁻²⁴ ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

**Q2. Why is the wave nature of a moving cricket ball (mass ≈ 0.15 kg) not observable?** Using λ = h/(mv), for even a small ball travelling at 30 m/s the wavelength is λ = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (0.15 × 30) ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻³⁴ m — far smaller than the size of a nucleus and completely unobservable; the wavelength is negligible for macroscopic objects (λ ∝ 1/m).

**Q3. If the uncertainty in the position of an electron is 10⁻¹⁰ m, what is the minimum uncertainty in its velocity?** Using Δx · Δv ≥ h/(4πm): Δv = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (4 × 3.14 × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 10⁻¹⁰) = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / 1.143 × 10⁻³⁹ ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m/s.

**Q4. Explain why Bohr's definite orbits contradict the uncertainty principle.** A definite orbit requires both position and momentum to be exactly known at every instant, but Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π forbids simultaneous exact knowledge — so the electron cannot follow a sharply defined circular path.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Q (worked examples): Atomic Number, Mass Number & Isotopes
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: **Q1. For the atom ₁₂Mg²⁴, find the number of protons, electrons and neutrons.** Atomic number Z = 12, so protons = 12 and electrons = 12 (neutral atom). Mass number A = 24, so neutrons = A − Z = 24 − 12 = 12.

**Q2. The magnesium ion Mg²⁺ has atomic number 12. How many protons and electrons does it contain?** Protons = Z = 12 (unchanged). Since the ion has lost 2 electrons, electrons = 12 − 2 = 10. Its atomic number remains 12.

**Q3. Protium (₁H¹), deuterium (₁H²) and tritium (₁H³) are isotopes. How do they differ?** All three have the same atomic number Z = 1 (one proton and one electron) but different mass numbers. Protium has 0 neutrons, deuterium has 1 neutron, and tritium has 2 neutrons. Protium is most abundant (99.98%), deuterium about 0.015%, and tritium only 10⁻¹⁵ % (radioactive).

**Q4. Show that ₁₈Ar⁴⁰, ₁₉K⁴⁰ and ₂₀Ca⁴⁰ are isobars.** All three atoms have the same mass number A = 40 but different atomic numbers (18, 19, 20). Hence they are isobars — atoms of different elements with the same mass number.

**Q5. Show that ₆C¹⁴, ₇N¹⁵ and ₈O¹⁶ are isotones.** For ₆C¹⁴: neutrons = 14 − 6 = 8. For ₇N¹⁵: neutrons = 15 − 7 = 8. For ₈O¹⁶: neutrons = 16 − 8 = 8. All have the same number of neutrons (8) but different atomic and mass numbers, hence they are isotones.

**Q6. Verify that ₁₉K³⁹ and ₉F¹⁹ are isodiaphers.** For ₁₉K³⁹: neutrons − protons = (39 − 19) − 19 = 20 − 19 = 1. For ₉F¹⁹: neutrons − protons = (19 − 9) − 9 = 10 − 9 = 1. Both have the same isotopic excess (1), hence they are isodiaphers.

class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.title: Self-Practice — Rutherford's Model Diagnostic Questions (Page 102)
class-11-notes/chemistry/atomic-structur.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: **Q1. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the nucleus of an atom contains the entire mass of the atom?** The fact that a minute fraction of alpha particles (about 1 in 20,000) were reflected back suffering a deflection of 180° shows that the nucleus must possess considerable mass — only a massive, dense centre could reflect alpha particles of considerable mass.

**Q2. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the central part (nucleus) of an atom is positively charged?** Some alpha particles (about 1 in 10,000) were deflected by as much as 90° or even larger angles. Since alpha particles are positively charged, they could only be repelled by a positively charged centre — proving the nucleus is positively charged.

**Q3. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the atom consists mostly of hollow or empty space?** The vast majority of alpha particles (about 99%) passed straight through the gold foil completely undeflected, showing that most of the space inside the atom is empty.

**Q4. What experimental evidence led Rutherford to conclude that the volume occupied by the nucleus is very small compared to the total volume of the atom?** Only a very small number of alpha particles (about 1 in 10,000) were deflected through 90° or larger angles, indicating that the positively charged centre (nucleus of radius 10⁻¹³ cm) occupies a tiny volume compared to the whole atom (radius 10⁻⁸ cm).

**Q5. Why did Rutherford select gold foil for the α-particle scattering experiment?** Gold can be beaten into an extremely thin sheet (0.00006 cm thickness), thin enough for alpha particles to pass through and interact with individual atoms; gold is also a heavy element with a highly charged nucleus, producing measurable deflections.

notes: This textbook page introduces Boyle's Law, which explains the mathematical relationship between the pressure and volume of a gas when temperature is held constant.
Here is a comprehensive summary of the core concepts, formula derivations, and significance shown on the page:
📜 Definition of Boyle's Law
• Statement: The volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure, provided the temperature remains constant.
• Core Concept: If you increase the pressure on a gas, its volume decreases proportionally. If you decrease the pressure, its volume increases.
🧮 Mathematical Derivation

P₁V₁ = K and P₂V₂ = K
4. General Equation:
P₁V₁ = P₂V₂
💡 Significance of Boyle's Law

• Gas Compressibility: It mathematically proves that gases are highly compressible. When you compress a gas (increase pressure), its molecules are pushed closer together, which directly increases its density.
• P-V Relationship: It establishes the fundamental baseline for how volume varies with changing external pressure.
Here is a breakdown of the remaining sections visible on the right-hand side of the page, which expand on the theory and real-world impact of Boyle's Law.
📉 Relation Between Density and Pressure
Boyle's Law can be rewritten to show how gas density changes with pressure at a constant temperature:
• The Formula: Density (d) is defined as mass divided by volume (d = m/V), meaning volume is inversely proportional to density (V = m/d).
• Substitution: Substituting this into Boyle's Law (P ∝ 1/V) yields:

• The Rule: At a constant temperature, the density of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its pressure. If you double the pressure, you pack twice as many gas molecules into the same space, doubling the density.
🚀 Practical Applications of Boyle's Law

• Syringes: When you pull the plunger of a syringe back, the volume inside increases, causing the internal pressure to drop. The higher atmospheric pressure outside pushes the liquid into the syringe.

• Breathing Mechanism: When you inhale, your diaphragm expands your lungs, increasing their volume. This lowers the internal air pressure, drawing outside air in. When you exhale, lung volume decreases, pressure increases, and air is pushed out.

• Scuba Diving: As a diver goes deeper underwater, the ambient pressure increases significantly. If a diver ascends too quickly while holding their breath, the decreasing water pressure causes the air trapped in their lungs to rapidly expand in volume, which can cause severe lung damage.

• High Altitude Behavior: At high altitudes, atmospheric pressure is low. Consequently, weather balloons or passenger aircraft cabins must account for the fact that gases expand dramatically under reduced external pressure.
