class-11-notes/physics/heat-and-temperat.title: HEAT AND TEMPERATURE — Chapter 9, Class 11 Physics (Concepts, All 5 Scales & Step-by-Step Numericals)
class-11-notes/physics/heat-and-temperat.topicTitle: HEAT AND TEMPERATURE — Chapter 9, Class 11 Physics (Concepts, All 5 Scales & Step-by-Step Numericals)
notes: 📘 TOPIC OUTLINE: Temperature vs Heat | Effects of Heat | Thermal Equilibrium & Zeroth Law | Thermometry | The 5 Temperature Scales & Fundamental Interval | General Conversion Formula | Numericals (Direct Conversion, Coincidence/Double-Reading Problems, Faulty Thermometer Problems, Arbitrary/Offset Scale Problems, Rate/Error Problems)

🌡️ TEMPERATURE — DEFINITION: Temperature is the average kinetic energy of all molecules present in a body. It tells you the DIRECTION heat will flow (hot → cold). Measured using a thermometer. SI unit: kelvin (K).

🔥 HEAT — DEFINITION: Heat is the SUM (total) of the kinetic energy of all molecules of a substance. It is a form of energy, measured in joules. Heat flows from a body at higher temperature to one at lower temperature until equilibrium is reached.

💡 KEY CONCEPTUAL DIFFERENCE (exam favorite): Temperature is an AVERAGE (intensive property — doesn't depend on amount of substance). Heat is a TOTAL/SUM (extensive property — depends on mass/amount). This is why a bucket of lukewarm water can contain MORE heat than a cup of boiling tea, even though its temperature is lower — more molecules means a bigger total, even if each molecule individually has less average energy.

⚡ EFFECTS OF HEAT: When heat is applied to a body, it can bring: (i) Change in temperature (ii) Change in volume (iii) Change of state of matter (iv) Electric effect (v) Generation of light energy (vi) Change in resistance.
⚖️ THERMAL EQUILIBRIUM: Two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when NO heat flows from one to the other after being brought into contact — meaning they are at the same temperature.

📐 ZEROTH LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS: If two systems are separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they must also be in thermal equilibrium with each other. (This law is what actually justifies using a thermometer — the thermometer is the 'third system'.)
🧪 THERMODYNAMIC SYSTEM: A system that can be described using thermodynamic parameters — Temperature, Pressure, Volume, and Heat exchange.
🔬 THERMOMETRY: The science of temperature and its measurement. THREE MAIN STEPS: (i) Construction (ii) Calibration (iii) Sensitiveness.
═══════════ SECTION A: THE 5 TEMPERATURE SCALES & FUNDAMENTAL INTERVAL ═══════════

💡 WHAT IS 'FUNDAMENTAL INTERVAL'? It is simply the NUMBER OF DIVISIONS between the Lower Fixed Point (LFP — ice/melting point) and Upper Fixed Point (UFP — steam/boiling point) on a scale. This single number is the KEY to comparing any two scales, because it tells you how 'coarse' or 'fine' each degree-step is. A bigger fundamental interval = smaller, finer degree-steps.
📝 TABLE A1 — ALL 5 TEMPERATURE SCALES

| Scale | Symbol | LFP (Ice Point) | UFP (Steam Point) | Fundamental Interval (UFP−LFP) | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Celsius | °C | 0 | 100 | 100 | Relative (0 = ice point) |
| Fahrenheit | °F | 32 | 212 | 180 | Relative (0 ≠ ice point) |
| Kelvin | K | 273 | 373 | 100 | Absolute (0 = absolute zero) |
| Réaumur | °R (Ré) | 0 | 80 | 80 | Relative (0 = ice point) |
| Rankine | °Ra | 491.67 | 671.67 | 180 | Absolute (0 = absolute zero) |

🔑 FEEL IT, DON'T MEMORIZE: Kelvin is just Celsius SHIFTED so 0 lands on absolute zero (same degree-SIZE as Celsius, fundamental interval 100). Rankine is just Fahrenheit SHIFTED so 0 lands on absolute zero (same degree-SIZE as Fahrenheit, fundamental interval 180). So Celsius↔Kelvin is a pure SHIFT (add 273), and Fahrenheit↔Rankine is also a pure SHIFT (add 459.67). But Celsius↔Fahrenheit needs both a SHIFT and a SCALE change (×9/5) because their degree-sizes differ.

📐 GENERAL CONVERSION FORMULA (works for ANY two scales, including Rankine): (Reading − LFP)/(Fundamental Interval) is the SAME fraction on every scale, because all scales measure the identical physical range between ice point and steam point.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE: Students often try converting Rankine using the Celsius-style formula (Ra−0)/x. WRONG — Rankine's zero is absolute zero, NOT the ice point, so you MUST use (Ra−491.67)/180, matching Fahrenheit's fundamental interval of 180, not Kelvin's 100.
═══════════ SECTION B: DIRECT CONVERSION NUMERICALS ═══════════
📝 NUMERICAL B1: Convert 30°C into Fahrenheit scale.
Step 2: Substitute C = 30: 30/100 = (F−32)/180
Step 3: Cross-multiply: 30×180/100 = F−32 → 54 = F−32
✅ ANSWER: 30°C = 86°F
📝 NUMERICAL B2: Convert 98.6°F (normal body temperature) into Kelvin and Rankine.
Step 2: Convert to Kelvin: K = C+273 = 37+273 = 310 K
Step 3: Convert to Rankine directly from Fahrenheit: Ra = F+459.67 = 98.6+459.67 = 558.27

💡 TIP: Kelvin was obtained from Celsius by pure ADDITION (+273), Rankine from Fahrenheit by pure ADDITION (+459.67) — no multiplication needed, since each absolute scale shares its degree-size with its 'parent' relative scale.
═══════════ SECTION C: 'DOUBLE READING' & 'COINCIDING SCALE' NUMERICALS (Concept-Challenging) ═══════════

📐 METHOD: These problems give a RELATIONSHIP between two scale readings (e.g. 'one is double the other' or 'both are equal') instead of a direct value. Assign a variable to the unknown common temperature, express both readings in terms of it using the given relationship, plug into the master equation, and solve.
📝 NUMERICAL C1: At what temperature will the Kelvin reading double the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let K = 2F
✅ ANSWER: At 176.69°F (353.38 K), Kelvin reading is double Fahrenheit reading.
📝 NUMERICAL C2: At what temperature will the Celsius reading double the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let F = x, so C = 2x
✅ ANSWER: At −12.307°F, Celsius reading is double Fahrenheit reading.
📝 NUMERICAL C3: At what point does the Kelvin reading coincide with (equal) the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let both = x
✅ ANSWER: At 574.25 K = 574.25°F, the readings coincide.
📝 NUMERICAL C4 (Concept-challenging — physically impossible case): At what temperature would the Rankine reading equal the Celsius reading numerically?
Step 1: Let both = x. Using Ra = 1.8(C+273): x = 1.8(x+273)
Step 3: Check against absolute zero (−273°C): −614.25°C is colder than absolute zero, so it cannot exist.
✅ ANSWER: No physically valid solution — the equality would require a temperature below absolute zero.
💡 TIP: ALWAYS sanity-check your final answer against absolute zero (−273°C / 0 K) when an absolute scale is involved — algebra can give you a number, but physics can reject it.
📝 NUMERICAL C5: At what temperature will the Réaumur reading be numerically equal to the Fahrenheit reading?
Step 1: Let both = x. x/80 = (x−32)/180
✅ ANSWER: At −25.6°Ré = −25.6°F, the readings coincide.
═══════════ SECTION D: FAULTY / MISCALIBRATED THERMOMETER NUMERICALS ═══════════

📐 METHOD: A faulty thermometer has WRONG numbers marked at its LFP and UFP, but still divides the space between them proportionally. Use: (Faulty reading − Faulty LFP)/(Faulty UFP − Faulty LFP) = (Correct reading − Correct LFP)/(Correct UFP − Correct LFP)
📝 NUMERICAL D1: A faulty thermometer has fixed points marked at 2 and 98 (instead of 0 and 100). What is the correct Celsius temperature when it reads 20°C?
✅ ANSWER: 18.75°C.
📝 NUMERICAL D2: A thermometer reads the melting point of ice as −10°C, and reads 60°C in place of the correct 50°C. Find its reading at the actual boiling point of water (100°C).
✅ ANSWER: The faulty thermometer reads 130°C at the true boiling point.
📝 NUMERICAL D3: The distance between LFP and UFP on a thermometer is 80 cm. Find the Celsius temperature when mercury has risen 10.4 cm above the LFP.
Step 1: 80 cm = 100°C, so 1 cm = 100/80 parts
✅ ANSWER: 13°C.
💡 TIP: This is the same ratio logic as the faulty-thermometer formula — physical stem length is just another 'scale' being converted into Celsius.
═══════════ SECTION E: ARBITRARY / OFFSET SCALE NUMERICALS (Concept-Challenging) ═══════════
📐 METHOD: These invent a new scale with its own LFP/UFP. Treat it exactly like Celsius vs Fahrenheit — set up the ratio, don't panic just because the scale is unfamiliar.
📝 NUMERICAL E1: In an arbitrary scale, water freezes at 40° and boils at 290°. Find the reading on this scale corresponding to 62°C.
Step 1: Arbitrary fundamental interval = 290−40 = 250
✅ ANSWER: 62°C corresponds to 195° on the arbitrary scale.
📝 NUMERICAL E2: A new scale 'X' has its ice point at −20°X and steam point at 130°X. Find the reading on X when Celsius reads 50°C.
Step 1: Fundamental interval of X = 130−(−20) = 150
✅ ANSWER: X = 55°X
📝 NUMERICAL E3 (two unknown scales, no Celsius needed): Thermometer P has LFP=10, UFP=160. Thermometer Q has LFP=20, UFP=120. When P reads 70, what does Q read?
✅ ANSWER: Q reads 60.
💡 TIP: Celsius is not mandatory as a 'bridge' — the ratio method works between ANY two linear scales directly.
📝 NUMERICAL E4: Scale 'Y' has the SAME fundamental interval as Celsius (100 divisions) but its ice point is marked at 50°Y. If Y reads 68°Y, find the Celsius equivalent.
Step 1: Equal fundamental intervals → pure shift relationship: C = Y−50
✅ ANSWER: 18°C.

💡 TIP: When two scales share the SAME fundamental interval, conversion is always pure addition/subtraction (like Celsius↔Kelvin) — no multiplication needed. Different fundamental intervals force a scaling step.
═══════════ SECTION F: RATE / ERROR / CHANGE NUMERICALS ═══════════
📝 NUMERICAL F1: A Fahrenheit thermometer reads 99°F when a standard Celsius thermometer reads 37°C. Find the error in the Fahrenheit scale.
Step 1: True Fahrenheit equivalent of 37°C: 37/100 = (F−32)/180 → 6660 = 100F−3200 → F = 98.6
✅ ANSWER: 0.4°F.
📝 NUMERICAL F2: A lab thermometer reads only in °F. Initial sample temperature is 68.2°F, and it must be increased by 40°C. Find the final temperature in °F.
Step 1: For a CHANGE (not absolute reading), use only the scaling ratio: 100 parts in °C = 180 parts in °F
Step 2: 40°C change = (180/100)×40 = 72°F change
✅ ANSWER: 140.2°F.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE: Never apply the full C-to-F formula (×9/5, +32) to a temperature CHANGE — the '+32' offset applies only to absolute readings. For a change, only the scaling factor (180/100) applies. This is the single most common error in this topic.
📝 NUMERICAL F3: A Celsius scale reads 30°C when a standard Kelvin scale reads 300 K. Find the error in the Celsius reading.
Step 1: True Celsius equivalent of 300 K: C = 300−273 = 27
Step 2: Error = 30−27 = 3
✅ ANSWER: 3°C.
📝 NUMERICAL F4: What are the temperatures in Celsius and Fahrenheit when 2/3 of the Fahrenheit reading equals 1/2 of the Celsius reading?
📝 NUMERICAL F5 (Rankine, concept-challenging): A gas thermometer shows a temperature change from 500°Ra to 680°Ra. Express this change in Celsius degrees.
Step 1: Rankine change = 680−500 = 180 Ra
Step 2: Since Rankine shares fundamental interval 180 with Fahrenheit, and Fahrenheit-to-Celsius scaling ratio is 100/180: Celsius change = 180×(100/180) = 100
✅ ANSWER: A 180°Ra change equals a 100°C change.

💡 TIP: This confirms the 'feel': Rankine degree-size = Fahrenheit degree-size, so converting a Rankine CHANGE to Celsius always goes through the F→C scaling ratio (100/180), never through the absolute-zero offset (491.67), since offsets cancel out in a difference.

🎯 QUICK SUMMARY OF ALL METHODS: (1) DIRECT CONVERSION between named scales → plug into the master equation (C−0)/100=(F−32)/180=(K−273)/100=(Ré−0)/80=(Ra−491.67)/180. (2) 'DOUBLE' or 'COINCIDE' problems → assign one variable to the unknown temperature, express both readings in terms of it, substitute into the master equation, and sanity-check against absolute zero. (3) FAULTY THERMOMETER problems → use (Faulty−FaultyLFP)/(FaultyUFP−FaultyLFP) = (Correct−CorrectLFP)/(CorrectUFP−CorrectLFP). (4) ARBITRARY/OFFSET SCALES → same ratio method; Celsius is not mandatory as a bridge. (5) CHANGE/DIFFERENCE in temperature → apply ONLY the scaling ratio between fundamental intervals, NEVER the additive offset.

1.9 Error in Measurement

There is a saying among craftsmen, 'Measure thrice, cut once.' This means that you can reduce the risk of making a mistake in the work by checking the measurement a second or third time before you proceed. In fact it is wise to make any measurement at least three times. Making only one measurement could go completely unnoticed.

Error: All the physical quantities are measurable so accurate measurement is an important part of physics. But the measured value of a physical quantity is usually different from its real value. In other words, we can never make measurements with all certainty and claim that measurements are hundred percent accurate because measurements with all certainty involve a certain error (or uncertainty). We can never take into account the neither instrument may be supposed to be perfect nor any experimenter may be perfect. Since you would not get the same value of x that you try to measure it, your result is obviously uncertain.
The numerical result of a complete measurement is then expressed in the form as
Numerical result = Measured value ± Error
Error = Measured value − Real value
The difference between the measured and the real values of a physical quantity is called error. It is also called uncertainty.
Here x̄ is the mean value of different values measured in the experiment.

For example, if the measured area of your book is 200 ± 0.2 cm². The ± 0.2 cm² ('plus or minus 0.2 cm²') denotes the error in the measurement. The real area of your book most likely lies between 200.2 cm² and 199.8 cm² i.e. the measurement is written as 200 ± 0.2 cm². The correct value of a quantity is not sure so we take the mean value as the correct or true value.
Numerical result = x̄ ± error
Here x̄ is the mean value of different values measured in the experiment.
How to Express an Error?
An error can be expressed by three ways:
(i) Absolute error
(ii) Relative error
(iii) Percentage error
Absolute error: The difference between real value and individual measured value of a physical quantity is called absolute error.
Absolute error = Real value − Measured Value
The correct value of a quantity is not sure so we take the mean value as the correct or real value.
Kinds of Error
Generally, errors in the measurement can be broadly classified into two categories:
(a) Random Errors
(b) Systematic Errors
(a) Random Error
The errors which are due to unknown causes are called random errors. They are also called accidental errors because they are not due to any definite cause.

Causes of Random Error: Random errors arise from the fluctuations that are most easily observed by making multiple trials of a given measurement. For example, if you were to measure the period of a pendulum with a stop watch, you would find that your measurements were not always the same. The main source of these fluctuations would probably be the difficulty of judging exactly when the pendulum came to a given point in its motion, and in starting and stopping the watch at that time. Since you would not get the same value of the period each time that you try to measure it, your result is obviously uncertain.

Minimization of Random Error: Systematic errors are generally 'simple' to analyze but random errors require a more careful judge. Experiments with very small random errors are said to have a high degree of precision. Random errors can be minimized by making a number of readings and then taking their mean.
(b) Systematic Error

The errors which are due to known causes are called systematic errors. The measurement is made under constant condition and hence the error repeats constantly or systematically. So, the error in this category belong to the same sign and always of the same magnitude of the instrument.
Causes of Systematic Error
Bias of the experimenter: Errors in the calibration of the measuring instruments. For example, one might make an incorrect reading because of parallax error.
Incorrect measuring technique: For example, the experimenter might consistently read an instrument incorrectly.

Systematic errors are errors that are constant and always of the same sign and thus may be reduced by averaging over a lot of data. Examples of systematic errors would be time constantly or systematically. So, the error belong to the same category of errors.

All instrumental errors belong to this category. All instrumental errors belong to the constancy of unit. Systematic errors are due to imperfections in the instrument and the imperfections of the instrument condition and hence the error repeats constantly or systematically. So, the error in this category belong to the same category.

Systematic errors are errors that are constant and always of the same sign, such as calibrated instruments. distance measurements by an inaccurately marked meter stick, faulty graduations of a Vernier Calipers and micrometer screw, the end error in a meter bridge, measuring scale etc.
Minimization of Systematic Error

Errors in the calibration of the measuring instruments. For example, one might make an incorrect scale reading because of an instrument incorrectly. Errors due to known causes are called systematic errors. The known causes are sources of errors. Systematic errors are not due to random causes but do not affect the precision of a measurement.

notes: Mean Value of a Set of Measurements
If A₁, A₂, ..... An be the values calculated in the measurement then their mean value as a real value is given by
Absolute Errors
Thus, absolute errors are given by
ΔA₁ = Ā − A₁
ΔA₂ = Ā − A₂
ΔAn = Ā − An
Mean Absolute Error
The mean absolute error is given by
$$\overline{\Delta A} = \frac{|\Delta A_1| + |\Delta A_2| + .... + |\Delta A_n|}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\Delta A_i| \quad ....(1.11)$$
When arithmetic mean is taken, only magnitudes of the absolute errors are taken into account.
Relative Error and Percentage Error
Relative error: The ratio of mean absolute error to the real value of the measured quantity is called relative error.
$$\text{Relative error} = \frac{\overline{\Delta A}}{\bar{A}} \quad ....(1.12)$$
If the relative error is expressed in percentage, then it is called percentage error. Obviously, the percentage error is simply the ratio of the error to the measured value, multiplied by 100%.
$$\text{Percentage error} = \frac{\overline{\Delta A}}{\bar{A}} \times 100\% \quad ....(1.13)$$
With the help of percentage error, we can judge the accuracy of the result.

Accuracy and Precision in Measurement

Accuracy is not the same as accuracy. Both accuracy and precision reflect how close a measurement is to an actual value, but accuracy reflects how close a measurement is to a known or accepted value, while precision reflects how reproducible measurements are, even if they are far from the accepted value.
The term 'Accuracy' denotes closeness of an experimental value to an experimental value of set or standard value.
Accuracy = Mean value − True value
Smaller the difference between the mean value and the true value, the larger is the accuracy.
For example, a student measured the mean value and he found the mean value 9.20 m/s². The standard value of g is 9.80 m/s²: Thus, accuracy = 9.80 − 9.20 = 0.60 m/s².

The accuracy of an instrument depends on how well its performance compares to a currently accepted standard. Uncertainties in measurement affect the accuracy of a measurement. Precision, however, is not affected because the accuracy depends on how well its performance compares to a currently accepted standard. The accuracy of an instrument is based on the accuracy of a measurement.

The term 'Precision' refers to how closely two or more measurements agree with one another. Precision is determined by the least count of the measuring instrument. The smaller the least count, the greater the precision.

For example, least count of Vernier calipers is often 0.01 cm and least count of a screw gauge is often 0.001 cm. So, measurement of small length using a screw gauge is more precise than a Vernier calipers.
Precision = individual value − mean value − Arithmetic mean value
In other words, precision gives the extent of agreement between the individual values of measurements.
This means that precision the difference between the individual values of repeated measurements, the smaller is the precision.
For example, a student was conducting an experiment to determine the value of g. He has taken many readings and the values are ranging from 9.80 m/s² to 9.802 m/s² with an average of 9.801 m/s².
Precision = least count of the measuring instrument. The smaller the least count, the greater the precision.
Thus, precision = 9.801 − 9.80 = 0.001 m/s².

notes: Introduction to Physics and Quantities
Physics is the branch of science that deals with natural phenomena at all scales, from subatomic particles to the entire universe. It deals with matter, energy, and the interactions between them.
The word Science originates from the Latin verb Scientia, meaning 'to know', representing systematically organized knowledge built on observations and experiments.

The term Physics is derived from the Greek word Physika, which means 'nature'. In Sanskrit, it is called Bhautika, which refers to the physical world, and an expert in this field is called a physicist.
Mathematics is considered the language of the universe, and physics heavily utilizes it as a powerful tool to describe basic laws of nature.
Branches of Mechanics
Mechanics is the branch of physics dealing with bodies either at rest or in motion.

• Statics: The branch of mechanics that deals with a body at rest.
  • Kinetics: The branch of mechanics that deals with a body in motion. It is further sub-divided into:
    • Kinematics: Derived from the Greek word kinema (meaning motion), it describes how objects move without taking into account the causes of that motion.
    • Dynamics: Derived from the Greek word dynamis (meaning power), it deals with why objects move as they do, acting as the general science of motion.
Particle vs. Body

• Particle (Point Object): A mathematical model of a mass point where its size (dimension) is negligible compared to another body or the distance involved (e.g., a football compared to a house).
  • Body: An object that possesses a certain size, mass, and volume.
Physical Quantities
Physical quantities are measurable quantities in terms of which the laws of physics are expressed. All physical quantities possess both a magnitude and a unit: Physical Quantity = Magnitude * Unit.
The numerical value N depends on the choice of unit U; a larger unit size results in a smaller numerical value, and vice versa. N is always positive.
Types of Physical Quantities

• Fundamental (Basic) Quantity: Quantities that do not depend on any other quantities. There are seven basic quantities: length, mass, time (Mechanics); illuminating power/luminous intensity (Optics); temperature (Heat); electric current (Electricity); and amount of chemical substance (Nuclear Physics). Sub-fundamental quantities include plane angle and solid angle.
  • Derived Quantity: Quantities obtained from fundamental quantities (e.g., Area, Density, Speed).
Measurement in Physics

Measurement is the process of comparing an unknown quantity with a known constant unit, determining the quantity of something. To measure a physical quantity, two things must be known: Unit and Numerical Value.

Principle of Measurement: The product of magnitude and unit always remains constant regardless of the system of units used (N * U = Constant or N1 * U1 = N2 * U2). Magnitude is inversely proportional to the scale of the unit.
Measurement provides objective observations identical for everyone. As stated by Lord Kelvin, knowledge is truly satisfactory only when expressed in numbers; measurement is the root of science.
Units of a Physical Quantity

A unit is a standard chosen quantity in terms of which a physical quantity is measured. It must be well-defined, convenient, easily reproducible, and independent of time, place, or physical conditions.
Fundamental Unit: A unit used to measure a fundamental quantity (e.g., kilogram, gram, meter).
Unit Classifications

• Non-Standard Units: Obscure units based on historical standards (e.g., firkin for volume, eon for time).
  • Hybrid Units: Combining units from two different measurement systems for a single physical quantity (e.g., ohm centimeter for resistivity).
Key Conversions

• 1 Fermi (femtometer): 10^-15 m (used for nuclear sizes)
  • 1 Angstrom: 10^-10 m
  • 1 Astronomical Unit (AU): 1.5 * 10^11 m
  • 1 Light Year: 9.5 * 10^15 m
  • 1 Parsec: 3.26 light years (3.08 * 10^16 m; largest practical unit of distance used for stars/galaxies)
  • 1 Litre: 10^-3 m^3
Dimensions of a Physical Quantity
The concept was introduced clearly by Joseph Fourier in 1822, though the foundational principle was known to Isaac Newton in 1686.
Definition: The dimensions of a physical quantity are the powers, indices, or exponents to which the base fundamental quantities must be raised to represent that quantity.
Base Representation: In mechanics, the fundamental quantities are represented by capital letters enclosed in square brackets, including Mass as M, Length as L, and Time as T.

Base Dimensional Symbols for all seven fundamental quantities: Length as L, Mass as M, Time as T, Temperature as K or theta, Electric Current as A or I, Amount of Substance as N, and Luminous Intensity as J.

• Dimensional Formula: An expression showing how and which basic quantities are involved in a derived physical quantity, usually written inside square brackets, such as Force equaling MLT to the power of -2.
  • Dimensional Equation: An equation obtained by equating a physical quantity with its dimensional formula.
  • Dimension vs. Unit: They are related but distinct. A physical quantity has only one unique dimensional formula, but its unit can differ across systems such as SI versus CGS.
  • Constants & Variables: Quantities can be dimensional constants like the universal gravitational constant G, dimensionless constants like pi, dimensional variables, and dimensionless variables.

Types of Physical Quantity

notes: Gateway of Knowledge

1. Often the certainty in a measured value is not specified explicitly. In such cases, the uncertainty is generally assumed to be one or two units in the last digit specified. For example, if a length is given as 6.2 cm, the uncertainty is assumed to be about 0.2 cm (or perhaps 0.1 cm). Here we assume that this implies an uncertainty of 0.01 cm, it assumes that it is probably between 6.19 cm and 6.21 cm, when actually we believe it is between 6.1 and 6.3 cm.
2. Error in sum and difference of quantities.
Let x = a + b. Then Δx = ±(Δa + Δb).
Similarly, let x = a − b. Then Δx = ±(Δa + Δb).
3. Error in product of quantities
Let x = a × b. Then Δx/x = ±(Δa/a + Δb/b)
4. Error in division of quantities
Let x = a/b. Then Δx/x = ±(Δa/a + Δb/b)
Example: Calculate uncertainty in percentage for the measurement 3.22

Answer: Generally, error in a measured value is not specified explicitly. In such cases, the error is assumed to be one or two units in the last digit specified. According to question uncertainty in measurement 3.22 so uncertainty is assumed to be 3.22 ± 0.01.
Measured value with uncertainty = 3.22 ± 0.01
Now % Uncertainty = Uncertainty/Measured value × 100% = 0.01/3.22 × 100% = 0.31%
1.10 Significant Figures (Digits)

In physics there are limits to the accuracy of measurement and its reliability. The simple way of expressing this reliability is by using Significant figures. In another way, the number of digits (figures) in a given number which we are reasonably sure about which we are reasonably sure are called significant figures. The more insignificant figure specified, the more precision than the next figure is implied.

For example, we suppose that the diameter of a rod is measured and its value is found to be 0.004mm. Here we feel that 4 is a reasonable value but we are not sure of the next figure. So we have indicated only one significant figure.
Rules to Determine the Number of Significant Figures to keep:

(i) All non-zero digits are significant figures. For example, 2365 has four significant figures. All zeros between two non-zero digits are significant figures. For example, 1003 has four significant digits.

(ii) All zeros to the right of last non-zero digits are not significant if they are not followed by a decimal point are not significant if they are not significant, then they are significant. For example, 2365 has four significant figures.
(iii) All zeros to the right of a decimal point but to the left of a non-zero digit are not significant. For example, 0.00356 has three significant digits.
(iv) All zeros to the right of a decimal point and also to the right of a non-zero digit are significant. For example, 0.07600 has four significant figures.
(v) All zeros to the right of the last non-zero digit after the decimal point are significant. For example, 4.00, 4.000, 4.0000 as per the requirement.
(vi) All zeros to the right of the last non-zero digit are significant only if they come from a measurement.

(vii) The exact numbers appearing in the mathematical formula of various physical quantities have infinite number of significant figures. For example, a square is given by 4 × side. Here, 4 is an exact number and has infinite significant figures.

(viii) Addition and subtraction: In adding or subtracting, the least significant figure of the sum or difference occupies the same relative position as the least significant figures of the quantities being added or subtracted. In this case the position that matters. For example, the sum of three masses 103.9 kg, 2.10 kg and 0.319 kg is 106.319 kg. This distance can be expressed as 202000 cm or 2.020×10⁵ cm or 2.020 Km.
(ix) Multiplication and Division: In multiplying or dividing, the final result should retain as many significant figures as are there in the original number with the least significant figures.

class-11-notes/physics/mechanics/concept.title: Vector
notes: Introduction

A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction and obeys the triangle law of addition. Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum. A scalar quantity has only magnitude. Examples: mass, time, temperature, speed, work.
Types of Vectors

Equal vectors: same magnitude and same direction. Negative vector: same magnitude, opposite direction. Null vector: zero magnitude (its direction is undefined). Unit vector: a vector of magnitude 1 along a given direction, written as $\hat{a} = \frac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}$. Parallel and antiparallel vectors: vectors along the same line (same or opposite sense). Position vector: vector joining the origin to a point. Collinear vectors: vectors along the same straight line.
Addition of Vectors — Triangle and Parallelogram Law
If two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ act at an angle $\theta$, the magnitude of their resultant $\vec{R} = \vec{a} + \vec{b}$ is:
$$R = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + 2ab\cos\theta}$$

and its direction is given by $\tan\alpha = \frac{b\sin\theta}{a + b\cos\theta}$, where $\alpha$ is the angle made by the resultant with $\vec{a}$. Special cases: parallel ($\theta = 0°$) gives $R = a + b$; antiparallel ($\theta = 180°$) gives $R = |a - b|$; perpendicular ($\theta = 90°$) gives $R = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
Resolution of Vectors
Any vector $\vec{A}$ can be resolved into two perpendicular components:
$$A_x = A\cos\theta, \quad A_y = A\sin\theta$$
with $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$ and $\tan\theta = \frac{A_y}{A_x}$. In unit vector notation, $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j}$.
Scalar (Dot) Product

$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = ab\cos\theta$. The result is a scalar. $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$ when the vectors are perpendicular. For unit vectors: $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i} = \hat{j}\cdot\hat{j} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{k} = 1$ and $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j} = 0$.
Vector (Cross) Product

$|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = ab\sin\theta$, directed perpendicular to the plane of the two vectors (right-hand rule). $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = 0$ when the vectors are parallel. The cross product is used for torque ($\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$) and angular momentum ($\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$).

class-11-notes/physics/mechanics/sets/di.title: Dimensional Analysis - Practice Set 1
notes: Q1. Find the dimensional formula of Force.
Solution: Force = mass × acceleration = mass × velocity/time = mass × (length/time)/time
Answer: [F] = [MLT⁻²]
Q2. Find the dimensional formula of Work and Energy.
Solution: Work = Force × Distance
Answer: [W] = [E] = [ML²T⁻²]
Q3. Find the dimensional formula of Power.
Solution: Power = Work/Time
Answer: [P] = [ML²T⁻³]
Q4. Find the dimensional formula of Pressure.
Solution: Pressure = Force/Area
Answer: [P] = [ML⁻¹T⁻²]
Q5. Using the principle of homogeneity, verify whether the equation v = u + at is dimensionally correct.
Solution:
Since both terms of R.H.S. have the same dimension [LT⁻¹], addition is valid.
Answer: The equation is dimensionally correct.
Q6. Check the dimensional correctness of s = ut + ½at².
Solution:
Both terms reduce to [L], and ½ is a dimensionless constant, so it doesn't affect the check.
Answer: [L.H.S.] = [R.H.S.] = [L]. The equation is dimensionally correct.
Q7. Check whether the equation for kinetic energy, KE = ½mv², is dimensionally correct.
Solution:
Answer: [L.H.S.] = [R.H.S.]. The equation is dimensionally correct.

class-11-notes/physics/mechanics/sets/di.title: Dimensional Analysis - Practice Set 2
notes: Q8. Using dimensional analysis, derive the formula for the time period (T) of a simple pendulum, given that T depends on its length (l), the acceleration due to gravity (g), and the mass of the bob (m).
Solution: Let T ∝ mᵃ lᵇ gᶜ, so T = K mᵃ lᵇ gᶜ, where K is a dimensionless constant.
Writing dimensions of each quantity:
Equating powers of M, L, and T:
Power of M: 0 = a
Power of T: 1 = −2c → c = −1/2
Power of L: 0 = b + c → b = 1/2
Substituting these values:
Answer: T = K√(l/g). Experimentally, K = 2π, giving the familiar formula T = 2π√(l/g). Note: this method cannot tell us the value of K (a limitation of dimensional analysis).
Q9. Derive an expression for the centripetal force (F) acting on a body of mass (m) moving with velocity (v) in a circle of radius (r), using dimensional analysis.
Solution: Let F ∝ mᵃ vᵇ rᶜ, so F = K mᵃ vᵇ rᶜ
Equating powers: a = 1 (mass); −b = −2 → b = 2 (time); b + c = 1 → c = 1 − 2 = −1 (length)
Answer: Experimentally K = 1, so F = mv²/r.
Q10. Convert 1 Joule into Erg using the dimensional method.
Solution: Dimensional formula of energy/work: [ML²T⁻²]
Joule is the SI unit, Erg is the CGS unit. Let 1 joule (N₁) = N₂ erg

SI SystemCGS System
NN₁ = 1N₂ = ?
MM₁ = 1 kgM₂ = 1 g
LL₁ = 1 mL₂ = 1 cm
TT₁ = 1 sT₂ = 1 s
Here a = 1, b = 2, c = −2 (from [ML²T⁻²])
$$N_2 = N_1 \left[\frac{M_1}{M_2}\right]^a \left[\frac{L_1}{L_2}\right]^b \left[\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right]^c$$
$$N_2 = 1 \times \left[\frac{1\,kg}{1\,g}\right]^1 \left[\frac{1\,m}{1\,cm}\right]^2 \left[\frac{1\,s}{1\,s}\right]^{-2}$$
Answer: 1 joule = 10⁷ erg.
Q11. Convert 1 Newton into Dyne using the dimensional method.
Solution: Dimensional formula of force: [MLT⁻²], so a = 1, b = 1, c = −2

SI SystemCGS System
NN₁ = 1N₂ = ?
M1 kg1 g
L1 m1 cm
T1 s1 s
$$N_2 = 1 \times \left[\frac{1\,kg}{1\,g}\right]^1 \left[\frac{1\,m}{1\,cm}\right]^1 \left[\frac{1\,s}{1\,s}\right]^{-2}$$
Answer: 1 newton = 10⁵ dyne.
Q12. Convert 1 erg into joule (reverse of Q10) and verify consistency.
Solution: Since 1 joule = 10⁷ erg, dividing both sides by 10⁷:
$$1\,\text{erg} = 10^{-7}\,\text{joule}$$
Answer: 1 erg = 10⁻⁷ joule. This confirms consistency with Q10.

Q13. Two students derive an equation for pressure exerted by a liquid column as P = kρgh, where ρ is density, g is gravitational acceleration, and h is height. Verify this is dimensionally correct with k = 1.
Solution:
Answer: [L.H.S.] = [R.H.S.]. The equation P = ρgh is dimensionally correct.
Q14. State a limitation of dimensional analysis, illustrated with an example.
Solution: Dimensional analysis cannot determine the value of a dimensionless constant appearing in a physical equation.

Example: In the equation T = k√(l/g) for a simple pendulum, k is a dimensionless numerical constant. Dimensional analysis correctly gives T ∝ √(l/g), but it cannot tell us that the experimental value of k is 2π. This value must be found through experiment or a full derivation, not dimensional methods alone.
Other limitations:
1. It cannot indicate whether a physical quantity is a scalar or a vector — e.g. dimensional formula of speed [LT⁻¹] doesn't reveal that speed is a scalar while velocity (same dimension) is a vector.
2. The relationship between more than three quantities involved in a physical phenomenon cannot be derived by the dimensional method, though its dimensional correctness can still be checked.

notes: Worked Example: Density Calculation with Significant Figures
Mass of an object is measured to be 4.237 kg (four significant figures) and its volume is measured to be 2.51 m³ (three significant figures), then its density is given by
$$\text{Density} = \frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Volume}} = \frac{4.237}{2.51} = 1.6880 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$$
Here 1.6880 kg m⁻³ has five significant figures but according to rule it should be expressed to only three significant figures i.e. 1.69 kg m⁻³.
One must remember that in general, the final result should not have more significant figures than the original data from which it was obtained.

Area of an object is measured to be (2.51 m³) as five significant figures but the least precise measurement must also be expressed to the 0.1 decimal place so our final result should be expressed to the 0.1 decimal place, giving us 106.3 kg.
But the least precise measurement is 103.9. This measurement is expressed to the 0.1 decimal place. Thus, the answer is rounded to the tenths place, giving us 106.319 kg = 106.3 kg.

Answer: 1 billion seconds = 1 × 10⁹ s
$$1 \times 10^9 \text{s} \times \frac{1\text{ h}}{3600\text{ s}} \times \frac{1 \text{ day}}{24 \text{ h}} \times \frac{1 \text{ y}}{365 \text{ day}} = 31.75 \text{ years}$$

class-11-notes/physics/optics/concepts/n.title: N1
notes: Sign Conventions for Spherical Mirrors
Standard Cartesian Convention
Think of the mirror as the center of a math graph. Left is negative, Right is positive. Up is positive, Down is negative.
Real images are always on the left and upside down → v is negative, m is negative.
Virtual images are always on the right and upright → v is positive, m is positive.
What Does "Real is Positive" (RIP) Mean?
Some textbooks use an alternative, non-Cartesian system called the "Real-is-Positive" (RIP) sign convention.
Distance rule: Distances to real things (real object, real focus, real image) are given a plus (+) sign.
Virtual rule: Distances to virtual things (virtual focus, virtual image) are given a minus (−) sign.
The catch: This rule applies strictly to distances (u, v, f), not to the magnification's orientation meaning. Even under RIP, a real image is still physically upside down.
Summary Comparison Table

Image NatureStandard ConventionReal-is-Positive (RIP) System
Real & Inverted−m (Negative)+m (Positive)
Virtual & Erect+m (Positive)−m (Negative)
Rule: In the RIP system, −m means a Virtual, Erect image. +m means a Real, Inverted image.
Magnification Formula Differs Between Systems
Standard Convention: m = −v/u
Real-is-Positive (RIP) System: m = v/u (the minus sign is dropped from the formula)
How the Sign of m is Determined in RIP
Because the formula is m = v/u, the sign of m depends entirely on whether the image is real or virtual:
Real Image: object distance (u) is real (+), image distance (v) is real (+). Therefore, m = +v/+u = Positive (+m).
Virtual Image: object distance (u) is real (+), image distance (v) is virtual (−). Therefore, m = −v/+u = Negative (−m).
The Core Point of Confusion
The confusion happens because the same physical image is described with completely opposite math signs depending on which system you choose.
Let's look at a Real, Inverted Image formed by a concave mirror: in the real world, the image is physically upside down and in front of the mirror.

FeatureStandard Cartesian SystemReal-is-Positive (RIP) System
Why it's namedBased on an X-Y graph axisBased on whether the light is real or fake
Object Distance (u)Negative (Left side of graph)Positive (Object is real)
Image Distance (v)Negative (Left side of graph)Positive (Image is real)
Focal Length (f)Negative (Left side of graph)Positive (Focus is real)
Magnification formulam = −v/um = v/u
Magnification signNegative (Because it points down)Positive (Because both v and u are positive)
How to Solve Problems Without Confusion
1. If your school uses the Standard System:

Think of the mirror as the center of a math graph. Left is negative, Right is positive. Up is positive, Down is negative. Real images are always on the left and upside down → v is negative, m is negative. Virtual images are always on the right and upright → v is positive, m is positive.
2. If your school uses the Real-is-Positive System:

Forget about the graph completely. Just ask: "Is this real or virtual?" Real images can be caught on a sheet of paper → v is positive, m is positive. Virtual images only look like they are inside the mirror → v is negative, m is negative.
Solved Numerical: Question 1

Problem: The radius of curvature of a convex mirror is 20 cm and it forms the image of an object kept on its principal axis, at a distance of 5 cm from the pole of the mirror. Find the distance of the object from the pole.
Solution:
Convex mirror radius of curvature (R) = +20 cm
Focal length (f) = R/2 = +20/2 = +10 cm
Convex mirrors always form virtual images behind the mirror, so image distance (v) = +5 cm
Answer: The object is at a distance of 10 cm from the pole.

class-11-notes/physics/optics/concepts/n.title: N2
notes: Part 1: Question Types & Their Solving Approaches
Every mirror problem falls into one of three main categories.
Type 1: The "Direct Finder"
What it is: The question gives you two variables (like u and f) and asks you to find the third (v), or asks for the final magnification.

Solving Approach: Write down the givens with correct signs. Use the mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u to find the missing distance. Use the magnification formula (m = −v/u or m = v/u) to find the image characteristics.
Type 2: The "Magnification Pivot"
What it is: The question gives you the focal length (or radius) and says the image is "n times magnified," but does not give you v.

Solving Approach: Express v in terms of u using the magnification formula (e.g., v = 3u or v = −3u). Substitute this expression into the mirror formula so that u is the only unknown variable. Crucial: if the question does not specify if the image is real or virtual, you must solve for both cases separately.
Type 3: The "Two-Position Shift"
What it is: The object is placed at one position, then moved to a second position.

Solving Approach: Step 1 (First Position) — use the first set of data to find the focal length (f) of the mirror; the mirror doesn't change, so f stays constant. Step 2 (Second Position) — use the newly found f along with the new position data to solve for the final target.
Part 2: The Hint Decoder (What Indicates What)
When reading a physics problem, specific words act as hidden codes.
1. Hints about the Mirror Type
"Shaving mirror" or "Makeup mirror" → It is a Concave mirror used to create an enlarged, virtual image.
"Rear-view mirror" or "Driver's mirror" → It is a Convex mirror used to see a wide view of smaller, virtual images.
"Reflecting surface is curved inwards" → Concave mirror.
"Reflecting surface is curved outwards" → Convex mirror.
2. Hints about Image Nature & Sign Rules

The Phrase in the QuestionStandard CartesianReal-is-Positive (RIP)
"Brought to a focus on a screen"Real Image → v negative, m negativeReal Image → v positive, m positive
"Inverted image"Real Image → v negative, m negativeReal Image → v positive, m positive
"Erect image" or "Upright"Virtual Image → v positive, m positiveVirtual Image → v negative, m negative
"Formed behind the mirror"Virtual Image → v positive, m positiveVirtual Image → v negative, m negative
"Formed in front of the mirror"Real Image → v negative, m negativeReal Image → v positive, m positive
Step 1: Find the Image Nature from the Keywords

If the question says......the Nature of the Image is
"Erect", "Upright", or "Behind the mirror"Virtual
"Inverted", "On a screen", or "In front of a concave mirror"Real
"Convex mirror" (for any real object)Always Virtual (and smaller)
"Magnified image by a convex mirror"Trick question! Convex mirrors cannot magnify
"Diminished image by a concave mirror"Always Real
Step 2: Choose the Sign Based on Your Convention
Option A: Standard Cartesian Convention (Most Common)
Real Image: Image is upside down (inverted) → take magnification as negative (−m). Image is in front of the mirror → take image distance as negative (−v).
Virtual Image: Image is upright (erect) → take magnification as positive (+m). Image is behind the mirror → take image distance as positive (+v).
Option B: Real-is-Positive (RIP) System
Real Image: real things get a plus sign → take magnification as positive (+m). Image is real → take image distance as positive (+v).
Virtual Image: virtual things get a minus sign → take magnification as negative (−m). Image is virtual → take image distance as negative (−v).
A Quick Example to Clarify
Question: "A concave mirror forms an image magnified 3 times on a screen."
1. Find Nature: the keyword "on a screen" means the image must be Real.
2. Apply Sign: In Standard Cartesian, take m = −3. In Real-is-Positive, take m = +3.
