questions.question: Why is the mitochondrion called the powerhouse of the cell?
questions.solution: Because it carries out **aerobic respiration** — the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation take place in it, producing most of the cell's ATP (energy currency). Hence it supplies energy for all cellular activities.

questions.question: Describe the economic importance of bacteria (any four points).
questions.solution:
**Useful roles of bacteria:**
1. **Dairy:** Lactobacillus converts milk into curd.
2. **Nitrogen fixation:** Rhizobium in root nodules of legumes enriches soil fertility.
3. **Medicine:** production of antibiotics and vaccines.
4. **Sewage treatment & biotechnology:** decomposition of waste; production of insulin by genetically engineered E. coli.

questions.question: What is a virus? Differentiate between DNA and RNA viruses with one example each.
questions.solution:
A **virus** is an acellular obligate intracellular parasite consisting of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) surrounded by a protein coat called capsid.

**DNA virus:** contains DNA as genetic material — e.g. Adenovirus, Poxvirus.

**RNA virus:** contains RNA — e.g. TMV (Tobacco Mosaic Virus), HIV, Influenza virus.

questions.question: State Miller–Urey experiment and its significance.
questions.solution:
In 1953 **Stanley Miller and Harold Urey** created a closed apparatus simulating the primitive Earth: they circulated CH₄, NH₃, H₂ and water vapour past electric sparks (simulating lightning) for a week.

Result: amino acids (glycine, alanine) and other organic compounds were formed.

**Significance:** it experimentally supported the **Oparin–Haldane theory of chemical evolution** — that life's building blocks could arise from non-living matter under primitive-Earth conditions.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a typical virus with a labelled description.
questions.solution:
A virus has:
- **Genetic material:** DNA or RNA (never both), either single or double stranded, at the centre.
- **Capsid:** protein coat made of capsomere units that protects the nucleic acid.
- **Envelope (in some):** outer lipoprotein layer derived from the host membrane.

Example — TMV is rod-shaped with ssRNA + helical capsid; bacteriophage T4 has a head (DNA), collar, sheath and tail fibres.

questions.question: Write the general characters of the phylum Arthropoda.
questions.solution:
**Arthropoda** (largest phylum of Animalia):
1. Body segmented, divided into head, thorax and abdomen.
2. Jointed paired appendages.
3. Chitinous exoskeleton that is moulted (ecdysis).
4. Open circulatory system; haemocoel present.
5. Compound eyes; tracheal/gill respiration.

Examples: Periplaneta (cockroach), Palaemon (prawn).

questions.question: Distinguish between in-situ and ex-situ conservation with examples.
questions.solution:
**In-situ conservation:** protecting species in their natural habitat — national parks, wildlife reserves, biosphere reserves (e.g. Chitwan National Park for one-horned rhino).

**Ex-situ conservation:** conserving species outside their natural habitat — zoos, botanical gardens, seed/sperm banks, tissue culture (e.g. captive breeding of gharial).

questions.question: What are the roles of Rhizobium bacteria in agriculture?
questions.solution: Rhizobium lives symbiotically in root nodules of leguminous plants and **fixes atmospheric nitrogen into usable nitrogenous compounds**, increasing soil fertility naturally. This reduces the need for chemical nitrogen fertilisers and forms the basis of crop rotation.

class-11/biology/theory/cell-biomolecule.title: Cell Biology & Biomolecules
notes: **Cell theory:** all living organisms are composed of cells; the cell is the structural and functional unit of life; all cells arise from pre-existing cells (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow).
**Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells:** prokaryotes lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (bacteria); eukaryotes have a nucleus and organelles such as mitochondria, ER, Golgi bodies.
**Mitochondrion:** powerhouse of the cell — site of aerobic respiration and ATP synthesis; has its own circular DNA (semi-autonomous organelle).

**Biomolecules:** carbohydrates (energy source; glucose C₆H₁₂O₆), proteins (made of amino acids joined by peptide bonds), lipids (fats/oils; concentrated energy store), nucleic acids (DNA/RNA carry hereditary information).
**Enzymes** are globular protein catalysts that speed up biochemical reactions by lowering activation energy; they are substrate-specific and work best at optimum temperature and pH.

class-11/biology/theory/faunal-evolution.title: Faunal Diversity, Evolution & Environment
notes: **Porifera (sponges):** pore-bearing aquatic animals with canal system; skeleton of spicules.
**Arthropoda:** largest phylum — jointed legs, chitinous exoskeleton, open circulatory system (insects, crabs).
**Chordata characters:** notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits and post-anal tail at some stage of life.

**Oparin–Haldane theory:** life originated from non-living organic molecules in the primitive reducing atmosphere ('primordial soup'); Miller–Urey experiment (1953) supported it by producing amino acids from CH₄, NH₃, H₂, H₂O with electric discharge.
**Darwinism:** natural selection — survival of the fittest; variations that help survival are inherited.

**Ecology levels:** organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome. Food chain shows energy flow; ~10% energy transfers to each trophic level. **Conservation:** in-situ (national parks) and ex-situ (zoos, seed banks).

class-11/biology/theory/floral-diversity.title: Floral Diversity & Microbiology
notes: **Binomial nomenclature** was introduced by Carolus Linnaeus — every organism gets two names: generic name + specific epithet (e.g. Mangifera indica).
**Five kingdom classification (Whittaker):** Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — based on cell structure, body organisation and nutrition.

**Algae:** chlorophyll-bearing, aquatic thalloid organisms; green algae (Spirogyra) have ribbon-shaped spiral chloroplasts; brown algae (Laminaria) have fucoxanthin; red algae (Polysiphonia) contain r-phycoerythrin.
**Bryophytes:** amphibians of the plant kingdom; need water for fertilisation; e.g. mosses and liverworts.
**Bacteria:** prokaryotic, reproduce by binary fission; useful forms fix nitrogen (Rhizobium) and ferment milk into curd (Lactobacillus).
**Virus:** acellular obligate parasite with DNA or RNA core and protein coat (capsid); e.g. TMV, HIV.
**Fungi:** heterotrophic, cell wall of chitin; yeast is unicellular and used in fermentation; Penicillium gives the antibiotic penicillin.

questions.question: Define mole. Calculate the number of moles in 44 g of CO₂.
questions.solution:
A **mole** is the amount of substance that contains as many elementary particles as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of C-12 (6.022 × 10²³ particles).

Molar mass of CO₂ = 12 + 32 = 44 g mol⁻¹.

n = mass/molar mass = 44/44 = **1 mole**.

questions.question: State Avogadro's law. What volume does 0.25 mole of a gas occupy at STP?
questions.solution:
**Avogadro's law:** equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

At STP, 1 mole occupies 22.4 L ⇒ 0.25 mole occupies 0.25 × 22.4 = **5.6 L**.

questions.question: An organic compound contains 40% carbon, 6.67% hydrogen and 53.33% oxygen by mass. Find its empirical formula (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16).
questions.solution:
Divide each % by atomic mass: C = 40/12 = 3.33; H = 6.67/1 = 6.67; O = 53.33/16 = 3.33.

Divide by the smallest (3.33): C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1.

**Empirical formula = CH₂O**.

questions.question: Distinguish between empirical and molecular formula with an example.
questions.solution:
The **empirical formula** gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound; the **molecular formula** gives the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule.

Example — benzene: molecular formula C₆H₆, empirical formula CH.

questions.question: State Dalton's atomic theory. What are its main drawbacks?
questions.solution:
**Dalton's postulates:** matter is made of indivisible atoms; atoms of the same element are identical in mass and properties; atoms of different elements differ; compounds form by combination of atoms in simple whole-number ratios.

**Drawbacks:** atom is divisible (electrons, protons, neutrons exist); isotopes of an element have different masses; it cannot explain complex ratios, isotopy or the nature of bonding.

questions.question: Write the electronic configuration of Fe (Z = 26) and Cr (Z = 24) and explain any anomaly.
questions.solution:
**Fe:** 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶.

**Cr:** 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹ 3d⁵.

**Anomaly:** chromium takes one electron from 4s into 3d to give a half-filled 3d⁵ configuration, which has extra stability due to symmetrical distribution and maximum exchange energy.

questions.question: Why is ionisation energy of nitrogen greater than that of oxygen?
questions.solution: Nitrogen has a half-filled stable 2p³ configuration, which requires more energy to remove an electron. In oxygen, removing one electron gives a more stable half-filled 2p³ arrangement, so less energy is needed — hence IE(N) > IE(O).

questions.question: Define hybridisation. What is the shape and bond angle of NH₃?
questions.solution:
**Hybridisation** is the intermixing of atomic orbitals of nearly equal energy to form an equal number of identical hybrid orbitals.

In NH₃ nitrogen is sp³ hybridised: one lone pair + three N–H bonds ⇒ **pyramidal shape**, bond angle **107°** (compressed from 109.5° by the lone pair).

questions.question: What is a limiting reagent? 2 g of hydrogen reacts with 32 g of oxygen to form water. Identify the limiting reagent and the mass of water formed.
questions.solution:
A **limiting reagent** is the reactant completely consumed in the reaction and which therefore limits the amount of product.

Reaction: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (4 g H₂ reacts with 32 g O₂).

Here only 2 g H₂ is available ⇒ H₂ is the **limiting reagent**.

4 g H₂ → 36 g H₂O, so 2 g H₂ → **18 g of water**.

questions.question: State Boyle's law and Charles' law. Write the ideal gas equation.
questions.solution:
**Boyle's law:** at constant temperature the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure (V ∝ 1/P).

**Charles' law:** at constant pressure the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (V ∝ T).

Combining with Avogadro's law gives the **ideal gas equation: PV = nRT**.

questions.question: Define oxidation number. Find the oxidation number of sulphur in H₂SO₄.
questions.solution:
**Oxidation number** is the charge an atom would have if electrons were transferred completely to the more electronegative atom.

In H₂SO₄: 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0 ⇒ S = +8 − 2 = **+6**.

questions.question: Why do real gases deviate from ideal behaviour?
questions.solution: At high pressure the volume occupied by gas molecules is no longer negligible compared with the container volume; at low temperature intermolecular attractions become significant. Both effects make PV ≠ nRT — hence real gases deviate most at high pressure and low temperature.

questions.question: Explain the shape of the water molecule using VSEPR theory.
questions.solution:
In H₂O, oxygen is sp³ hybridised with **two bond pairs and two lone pairs**.

According to VSEPR, lone pair–lone pair repulsion is greater than lone pair–bond pair repulsion, which compresses the tetrahedral angle from 109.5° to about **104.5°**.

Hence the shape of H₂O is **bent (angular or V-shaped)**.

questions.question: Define ionisation energy. Why does it increase across a period?
questions.solution:
**Ionisation energy** is the minimum energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom.

Across a period nuclear charge increases while the shell number stays the same, so electrons are held more strongly — more energy is needed to remove them. Hence IE increases across a period.

questions.question: What are isotopes? Give one example.
questions.solution:
**Isotopes** are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different mass numbers (different numbers of neutrons).

Example: protium (¹₁H), deuterium (²₁H) and tritium (³₁H) — isotopes of hydrogen; also ¹²C and ¹⁴C.

questions.question: Write a short note on Graham's law of diffusion.
questions.solution:
**Graham's law:** at constant temperature and pressure, the rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass: r ∝ 1/√M, so r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁).

Lighter gases diffuse faster — e.g. hydrogen diffuses about four times faster than oxygen.

questions.question: State Le Chatelier's principle. Predict the effect of increasing pressure on N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
questions.solution:
**Le Chatelier's principle:** when a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that minimises the disturbance.

For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ there are 4 moles of gas on the left and only 2 on the right. Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium **towards the right (more ammonia)**, since fewer gas molecules means lower pressure.

questions.question: Calculate the pH of a 0.001 M HCl solution.
questions.solution:
HCl is a strong acid and dissociates completely: [H⁺] = 0.001 = 10⁻³ M.

pH = −log[H⁺] = −log(10⁻³) = **3**.

questions.question: What is a coordinate (dative) bond? Give an example.
questions.solution:
A **coordinate bond** is a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is donated by only one of the two bonded atoms (the donor), the other being the acceptor.

Example: NH₄⁺ — nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺; also H₃O⁺.

questions.question: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer.
questions.solution:
**Oxidation** is the loss of electrons by an atom/ion (increase in oxidation number). **Reduction** is the gain of electrons (decrease in oxidation number).

Example: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction).

questions.question: State Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and give its significance.
questions.solution:
**Heisenberg's uncertainty principle:** it is impossible to determine simultaneously and exactly both the position and the momentum of a moving microscopic particle.

Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π.

**Significance:** it rules out fixed orbits for electrons (contradicting Bohr) and leads to the concept of orbitals — regions of probability of finding the electron.

questions.question: What is the de Broglie equation? Calculate the wavelength of an electron moving at 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).
questions.solution:
The **de Broglie equation** λ = h/mv relates the wave nature to the particle nature of matter.

λ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 10⁶)

= 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ / 9.1 × 10⁻²⁵ ≈ **7.28 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 0.728 nm**.

questions.question: Why are noble gases chemically inert? Explain with reference to their electronic configuration.
questions.solution: Noble gases have completely filled outermost shells (ns² np⁶, except helium 1s²), giving maximum stability. They neither need to lose nor gain electrons, so they have high ionisation energy, almost zero electron affinity and very low reactivity.

questions.question: Distinguish between sigma (σ) and pi (π) bonds.
questions.solution:
**Sigma bond:** formed by head-on (axial) overlap of orbitals; stronger; free rotation possible; only one σ bond between two atoms.

**Pi bond:** formed by sidewise (lateral) overlap of p-orbitals; weaker; rotation restricted; always present along with a σ bond (in double/triple bonds).

questions.question: Define molarity. Calculate the molarity of a solution containing 4 g of NaOH in 500 mL of solution.
questions.solution:
**Molarity (M)** is the number of moles of solute dissolved per litre of solution.

Moles of NaOH = 4/40 = 0.1 mol. Volume = 500 mL = 0.5 L.

M = 0.1 / 0.5 = **0.2 M**.

questions.question: What is sp³ hybridisation? Explain the structure of methane using it.
questions.solution:
In **sp³ hybridisation** one s orbital and three p orbitals of comparable energy mix to form four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedrally at 109°28′.

In CH₄, carbon's one 2s electron is promoted to 2p, giving four unpaired electrons which hybridise into four sp³ orbitals; each overlaps with a hydrogen 1s orbital forming four identical C–H bonds — hence CH₄ is **tetrahedral with bond angle 109.5°**.

questions.question: State Pauli's exclusion principle and Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity.
questions.solution:
**Pauli exclusion principle:** no two electrons in the same atom can have all four quantum numbers identical — an orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins.

**Hund's rule:** electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins before pairing begins, because this arrangement has maximum stability (maximum multiplicity).

questions.question: Why is BF₃ non-polar while NF₃ is polar?
questions.solution:
BF₃ is trigonal planar and symmetrical: the three B–F bond dipoles cancel exactly ⇒ net dipole moment is zero ⇒ **non-polar**.

NF₃ is pyramidal (lone pair on N): the N–F bond dipoles do not cancel ⇒ net dipole moment exists ⇒ **polar**.

questions.question: What is a functional group? Write the general formula of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes.
questions.solution:
A **functional group** is an atom or group of atoms that determines the characteristic chemical properties of an organic compound (e.g. –OH, –CHO, –COOH).

Alkanes: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; Alkenes: CₙH₂ₙ; Alkynes: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.

questions.question: Define isomerism. Draw the chain isomers of C₅H₁₂ and name them.
questions.solution:
**Isomerism** is the phenomenon in which compounds have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements (and hence different properties).

Chain isomers of C₅H₁₂ (pentane):
1. **n-pentane** — CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃
2. **isopentane (2-methylbutane)** — (CH₃)₂CH–CH₂–CH₃
3. **neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane)** — C(CH₃)₄

questions.question: Explain why the bond angle in NH₃ is greater than that in H₂O.
questions.solution:
NH₃ has one lone pair, H₂O has two. Lone pair–lone pair repulsion is stronger than lone pair–bond pair repulsion.

In H₂O the two lone pairs compress the angle more (104.5°) than the single lone pair does in NH₃ (107°). Hence **angle(NH₃) > angle(H₂O)**.

questions.question: Balance the following redox equation by ion-electron method: Fe²⁺ + MnO₄⁻ → Fe³⁺ + Mn²⁺ (acidic medium).
questions.solution:
Oxidation: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ …(×5)

Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O

Adding: **5Fe²⁺ + MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ → 5Fe³⁺ + Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O**

questions.question: State the law of multiple proportions and explain it with an example.
questions.solution:
**Law:** when two elements combine to form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio.

Example — carbon and oxygen form CO and CO₂. With 12 g carbon: 16 g oxygen in CO, but 32 g in CO₂. Ratio = 16 : 32 = **1 : 2**.

questions.question: What is the significance of quantum numbers? Write the four quantum numbers for the differentiating (19th) electron of potassium (Z = 19).
questions.solution:
**Significance:** principal quantum number (n) gives size/energy of shell; azimuthal (l) gives shape of orbital; magnetic (m_l) gives orientation; spin (m_s) gives spin direction. Together they completely describe an electron in an atom.

Configuration of K: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ **4s¹** — the 19th electron:

n = 4, l = 0, m_l = 0, m_s = +½.

questions.question: Why does the boiling point of water differ from that of H₂S despite both having similar molecular structures?
questions.solution: Water molecules are held together by strong **hydrogen bonds** due to the high electronegativity and small size of oxygen, so much more energy is needed to separate them. In H₂S there is no hydrogen bonding (sulphur is large and less electronegative) — only weak van der Waals forces. Hence H₂O boils far higher (100 °C) than H₂S (−60 °C).

questions.question: Define molar volume. What volume will 8 g of methane occupy at STP?
questions.solution:
**Molar volume** is the volume occupied by one mole of any gas at STP (= 22.4 L mol⁻¹).

Moles of CH₄ = 8/16 = 0.5 mol ⇒ V = 0.5 × 22.4 = **11.2 L**.

questions.question: What is the octet rule? What are its limitations?
questions.solution:
**Octet rule:** atoms tend to combine in such a way that each has eight electrons in its valence shell, attaining noble-gas configuration.

**Limitations:**
- Incomplete octet: BeCl₂, BF₃ (central atom has only 4/6 electrons).
- Expanded octet: SF₆, PCl₅ (10 or 12 electrons around central atom).
- Odd-electron molecules: NO, NO₂ cannot satisfy the rule.
- It says nothing about shape, relative stability or energy of molecules.

questions.question: Calculate the number of molecules and moles present in 5.6 L of oxygen gas at STP.
What is a homologous series? State any two characteristics.
questions.solution:
A **homologous series** is a family of organic compounds with the same general formula, same functional group and similar chemical properties, whose successive members differ by –CH₂– unit.

**Characteristics:** (i) members can be prepared by similar methods; (ii) physical properties change gradually with molecular mass; (iii) consecutive members differ by 14 in molecular mass.

questions.question: Why is the electron affinity of chlorine higher than that of fluorine?
questions.solution: Fluorine's valence shell (2p) is very compact — an incoming electron feels strong repulsion from the already present electrons. Chlorine's 3p shell is larger, so the added electron experiences much less repulsion despite lower electronegativity. Hence Cl has a **higher (more negative) electron affinity** than F.

class-11/chemistry/theory/atomic-structu.title: Atomic Structure
notes: **Dalton's atomic theory:** matter consists of indivisible atoms; atoms of an element are identical in mass and properties; compounds form by combination of atoms in fixed ratios.

**Sub-atomic particles:** electron (e⁻, discovered by J.J. Thomson, charge −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass ≈ 1/1837 u); proton (p⁺, Goldstein/Rutherford, +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 1 u); neutron (n, Chadwick, neutral, 1 u).

**Bohr's model:** electrons revolve in fixed circular orbits (stationary states) with quantised angular momentum mvr = nh/2π; energy is emitted/absorbed only when an electron jumps between orbits: ΔE = hν. Radius rₙ = 0.529 n²/Z Å; energy E_n = −13.6 Z²/n² eV.

**Defects of Bohr's model:** cannot explain spectra of multi-electron atoms, fine structure (splitting of spectral lines), Zeeman and Stark effects, and the dual nature/wave character of the electron (de Broglie) or Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.

**Quantum numbers:** principal (n), azimuthal (l = 0 … n−1: s, p, d, f), magnetic (m_l = −l … +l) and spin (m_s = ±½). **Pauli exclusion:** no two electrons in an atom have identical sets of four quantum numbers. **Hund's rule** and Aufbau principle govern filling order.

class-11/chemistry/theory/chemical-bondi.title: Chemical Bonding & Shapes of Molecules (VSEPR)
notes: **Ionic bond:** electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed by transfer of electrons (e.g. NaCl). High melting point, conducts electricity in molten/solution state.
**Covalent bond:** mutual sharing of electron pairs (e.g. H₂, CH₄). Directional; low melting/boiling point compared with ionic solids.
**Coordinate (dative) bond:** shared pair donated by one atom only (e.g. NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺).

**VSEPR theory:** electron pairs around the central atom repel each other and arrange to be as far apart as possible. Repulsion order: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.

Shapes: AX₂ linear (BeCl₂), AX₃ trigonal planar (BF₃), AX₄ tetrahedral (CH₄), AX₃E pyramidal (NH₃, 107°), AX₂E₂ bent (H₂O, 104.5°), AX₅ trigonal bipyramidal (PCl₅), AX₆ octahedral (SF₆).

**Hybridisation:** intermixing of orbitals of comparable energy to form equivalent hybrid orbitals — sp (linear, 180°), sp² (trigonal planar, 120°), sp³ (tetrahedral, 109.5°), sp³d (trigonal bipyramidal), sp³d² (octahedral).

class-11/chemistry/theory/equilibrium-or.title: Chemical Equilibrium & Organic Fundamentals
notes: **Chemical equilibrium:** the stage at which rate of forward reaction equals rate of backward reaction; concentrations remain constant. Dynamic in nature.
**Le Chatelier's principle:** if a system at equilibrium is disturbed by changing concentration, pressure or temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that opposes the change.
**Equilibrium constant K_c** = [products]^coeff / [reactants]^coeff. For gas reactions K_p = K_c(RT)^Δn.
**Acids & bases (Bronsted-Lowry):** acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor. pH = −log[H⁺]; pH + pOH = 14.

**Organic chemistry basics:** catenation, tetravalency of carbon, homologous series, functional groups, isomerism (chain, position, functional), IUPAC nomenclature rules for alkanes/alkenes/alkynes and simple derivatives.

class-11/chemistry/theory/oxidation-redu.title: Oxidation, Reduction & Redox Reactions
notes: **Oxidation:** loss of electrons / gain of oxygen / increase in oxidation number. **Reduction:** gain of electrons / loss of oxygen / decrease in oxidation number.
**Oxidising agent** accepts electrons (is reduced); **reducing agent** donates electrons (is oxidised).

**Oxidation number rules:** free element = 0; monatomic ion = its charge; O is usually −2 (−1 in peroxides); H is +1 with non-metals and −1 with metals; the sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral molecule is 0.
**Balancing redox equations** — ion-electron (half-reaction) method or oxidation-number method; in acidic medium balance O with H₂O and H with H⁺.
**Applications:** electrochemical cells, electrolysis, corrosion, bleaching and titrations (redox titrations of KMnO₄/K₂Cr₂O₇).

class-11/chemistry/theory/periodic-table.title: Periodic Table & Periodicity
notes: **Modern periodic law:** properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers. The long form of the periodic table has 7 periods and 18 groups.

**Periodic trends:**
- **Atomic radius** decreases across a period (increasing nuclear charge) and increases down a group (new shells added).
- **Ionisation energy** increases across a period, decreases down a group.
- **Electronegativity** increases across a period, decreases down a group.
- **Electron affinity** generally increases across a period.
- **Metallic character** decreases across a period and increases down a group.
**Anomalies:** Be > B and N > O in ionisation energy due to extra stability of fully/half-filled sub-shells (1s², 2s², 2p³).
**Diagonal relationship:** elements of period 2 (Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si) resemble the diagonal element of period 3 in properties.

class-11/chemistry/theory/states-of-matt.title: States of Matter (Gaseous State)
notes: **Boyle's law:** at constant T, V ∝ 1/P. **Charles' law:** at constant P, V ∝ T. **Avogadro's law:** equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules at same T and P.
**Ideal gas equation:** PV = nRT, R = 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

**Kinetic theory of gases:** molecules are in continuous random motion; collisions are perfectly elastic; volume of molecules is negligible compared with the container; no intermolecular attraction; average KE ∝ absolute temperature.
**Graham's law of diffusion:** rate of diffusion ∝ 1/√(molar mass).
**Real gases** deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature; van der Waals equation corrects for molecular volume and attraction.

class-11/chemistry/theory/stoichiometry..title: Basic Concepts of Chemistry & Stoichiometry
notes: **Mole:** the amount of substance containing as many particles (atoms, molecules, ions) as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12. One mole = **6.022 × 10²³** particles (Avogadro's number, N_A).
**Molar mass:** mass of one mole of a substance in grams; numerically equal to its molecular/atomic weight. n = given mass / molar mass.
**Laws of chemical combination:** law of conservation of mass, law of definite (constant) proportions, law of multiple proportions and Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes.
**Empirical formula** gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; **molecular formula** = n × empirical formula where n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass.
**Limiting reagent:** the reactant that is completely consumed first and therefore limits the amount of product formed.
**Percentage yield:** (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100.

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Law of Conservation of Mass — Statement
notes: **Statement:** matter (mass) can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction — the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products
This is why chemical equations must be balanced: the same total mass, and the same number of each type of atom, must appear on both sides

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Law of Definite (Constant) Proportions — Statement
notes: **Statement:** a given chemical compound always contains its constituent elements combined together in the same fixed proportion by mass, regardless of the source of the compound or the method used to prepare it
This is verified experimentally by checking that the percentage composition of an element stays constant across independently prepared samples of the same compound

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Law of Multiple Proportions — Statement
notes: **Statement:** when two elements combine to form more than one compound, the different masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other element are in a ratio of small whole numbers
This is verified by finding the mass of one element that combines with a fixed mass (e.g. 1 g) of the other element in each compound, then comparing those masses as a ratio

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Law of Reciprocal Proportions — Statement
notes: **Statement:** when two different elements combine separately with a fixed mass of a third element, the ratio of the masses in which they do so is either the same as, or a simple whole-number multiple of, the ratio of masses in which the two elements combine directly with each other

This is verified by finding (i) the mass of each of the two elements that combines with a fixed mass of the third element (in two separate compounds), and (ii) the actual ratio of those two elements in a compound where they combine directly — then comparing the two ratios

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Law of Multiple Proportions — Verifying a Simple Whole-Number Ratio
notes: **Step 1 — divide by the smallest value:** take the calculated list of masses (or mass ratios), pick the smallest one, and divide every value in the list by it — this forces the smallest value to become exactly 1

**Step 2 — clear any remaining decimals:** if a result still ends in .5, .33/.66, or .25/.75, multiply every value in the list by a common factor to clear it — ×2 for .5, ×3 for .33/.66, ×4 for .25/.75 — until all values are whole numbers
**Alternative for already-whole numbers:** find the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of the numbers and divide each by it — e.g. 12:16 → HCF = 4 → 3:4

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Q: 12 g of carbon reacts with 32 g of hydrogen to produce 44 g of methane — which chemical law do these data illustrate?
notes: Reactants: carbon (12 g) + hydrogen (32 g)
Total mass of reactants = 12 + 32 = 44 g
Total mass of product (methane) = 44 g
Since the mass before the reaction (44 g) equals the mass after (44 g), mass is neither created nor destroyed
**Answer: this illustrates the Law of Conservation of Mass**

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Q: 20 g of CaCO₃ is heated and produces 11.2 g of CaO — calculate the weight of CO₂ produced
notes: Reaction: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
By the Law of Conservation of Mass: mass of CaCO₃ = mass of CaO + mass of CO₂
20 g = 11.2 g + mass of CO₂
**Answer: mass of CO₂ = 20 − 11.2 = 8.8 g**

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Q: 6.3 g of NaHCO₃ added to 10 g of HCl solution leaves a 12 g residue — what is the mass of CO₂ released?
notes: Reaction: NaHCO₃ + HCl → Residue + CO₂↑
Total mass of reactants: 6.3 g (NaHCO₃) + 10 g (HCl) = 16.3 g
By the Law of Conservation of Mass: total mass of reactants = total mass of products
16.3 g = 12 g + mass of CO₂
**Answer: mass of CO₂ = 16.3 − 12 = 4.3 g**

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Q: Two samples of common salt contain different masses of chlorine — show these results agree with the law of constant proportion
notes: **Data:** 0.25 g of sample 1 contains 0.1518 g of chlorine; 0.24 g of sample 2 contains 0.1458 g of chlorine
Since the percentage of chlorine is nearly identical in both samples (≈ 60.7%), regardless of sample size, this confirms the **Law of Constant (Definite) Proportion**

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Q: Two copper oxide reduction experiments — show they illustrate the law of definite proportions
notes: **Experiment 1:** 1.375 g of CuO is reduced to 1.098 g of copper by dry hydrogen gas
**Experiment 2:** 1.179 g of metallic copper is formed from 1.476 g of copper oxide
The percentage of copper is essentially constant (≈ 79.9%) across both experiments, verifying the **Law of Definite Proportions**

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Q: Determine the weight of oxide formed by heating 1 g of a carbonate (using the law of definite proportions)
notes: **Data:** 0.36 g of a metal burnt in oxygen yields 0.60 g of oxide; the carbonate of that metal contains 28.57% of the metal
From the oxide experiment: mass of metal = 0.36 g, mass of oxide = 0.60 g → ratio (mass of metal)/(mass of oxide) = 0.36/0.60 = **0.6**
From the carbonate experiment: 1 g of carbonate contains 28.57% metal → mass of metal in 1 g carbonate = 0.2857 g
By the Law of Definite Proportions, the metal-to-oxide ratio stays fixed at 0.6, so: 0.2857 / (mass of oxide) = 0.6
Mass of oxide = 0.2857 / 0.6
**Answer: mass of oxide = 0.4762 g**

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Q: Hydrogen and oxygen react separately to give H₂O₂ and H₂O — what law of stoichiometry is illustrated?
notes: Two elements (hydrogen and oxygen) combine to form more than one compound: H₂O and H₂O₂
For a fixed mass of hydrogen (2 g), the masses of oxygen that combine are 16 g (in H₂O) and 32 g (in H₂O₂)
Ratio of oxygen masses = 16 : 32 = **1 : 2** — a simple whole-number ratio
**Answer: this illustrates the Law of Multiple Proportions**

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Q: A metal forms two oxides (11.9% and 21.2% oxygen) — show these data illustrate the law of multiple proportions
notes: Oxide 1: oxygen = 11.9%, metal = 100 − 11.9 = 88.1% → mass of oxygen combined with 1 g of metal = 11.9/88.1 = **0.135 g**
Oxide 2: oxygen = 21.2%, metal = 100 − 21.2 = 78.8% → mass of oxygen combined with 1 g of metal = 21.2/78.8 = **0.269 g**
Ratio of oxygen combining with a fixed mass (1 g) of metal: 0.135 : 0.269 ≈ **1 : 2**
Since 1:2 is a simple whole-number ratio, this confirms the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Q: Element X forms three binary compounds with chlorine (50.08%, 66.73%, 74.95% Cl) — show how these illustrate the law of multiple proportions
notes: Compound 1: Cl = 50.08%, X = 49.92% → mass of Cl per gram of X = 50.08/49.92 = **1.003 g**
Compound 2: Cl = 66.73%, X = 33.27% → mass of Cl per gram of X = 66.73/33.27 = **2.006 g**
Compound 3: Cl = 74.95%, X = 25.05% → mass of Cl per gram of X = 74.95/25.05 = **2.992 g**
Ratio of chlorine masses combining with a fixed mass of X: 1.003 : 2.006 : 2.992 ≈ **1 : 2 : 3**
The simple whole-number ratio confirms the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Q: Four hydrocarbons with % compositions (C 75%/H 25%, C 80%/H 20%, C 85.7%/H 14.3%, C 92.3%/H 7.7%) — prove the law of multiple proportions
notes: Find the mass of hydrogen combining with a fixed mass (1 g) of carbon in each: (a) 25/75 = 0.333 g; (b) 20/80 = 0.250 g; (c) 14.3/85.7 = 0.167 g; (d) 7.7/92.3 = 0.083 g
**Ratio of hydrogen masses = 4 : 3 : 2 : 1**
This simple whole-number ratio proves the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Q: Three oxides of lead reduced in hydrogen — show this illustrates the law of multiple proportions
notes: **Data:** (i) 1.393 g of litharge gave 1.293 g of lead; (ii) 2.173 g of lead peroxide gave 1.882 g of lead; (iii) 1.712 g of red lead gave 1.552 g of lead
Find the mass of oxygen in each oxide by subtracting the lead mass from the total oxide mass: (i) 1.393 − 1.293 = 0.100 g; (ii) 2.173 − 1.882 = 0.291 g; (iii) 1.712 − 1.552 = 0.160 g
Find the mass of Pb combining with 1 g of O in each: (i) 1.293/0.100 = 12.93 g; (ii) 1.882/0.291 = 6.467 g; (iii) 1.552/0.160 = 9.700 g
Ratio: 12.93 : 6.467 : 9.700 — dividing all terms by 6.467 gives 2 : 1 : 1.5
Clearing the decimal by multiplying by 2: **4 : 2 : 3**
This simple whole-number ratio validates the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

class-11/chemistry/unit-2-stoichiometry/.title: Q: Nitrogen forms five oxides with oxygen (0.572 g, 1.14 g, 1.73 g, 2.28 g, 2.85 g of O per 1.09 g of N) — show how these illustrate the law of multiple proportions
notes: Fixed mass of nitrogen = 1.09 g in all five oxides
**Ratio of oxygen masses = 1 : 2 : 3 : 4 : 5**
This simple whole-number ratio illustrates the **Law of Multiple Proportions**

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Rutherford's Atomic Model — The Alpha-Particle Scattering Experiment
notes: **Experiment:** positively charged helium ions (α-particles) were fired at an ultra-thin gold foil
**Observation:** most α-particles passed straight through, undeflected
**Conclusion:** atoms are mostly empty space, with a tiny, dense, positively charged core called the **nucleus**

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Rutherford's Atomic Model — The Stability Crisis (Flaw)
notes: According to classical electromagnetic theory, any accelerating charged particle — such as an electron moving in a circular orbit — must continuously radiate energy
If the electron continuously loses energy, it should spiral inward and eventually collapse into the nucleus
Rutherford's model gave no explanation for why atoms are actually stable and this collapse does not happen — this is the model's central defect

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Postulates
notes: Niels Bohr resolved Rutherford's stability problem by introducing Planck's Quantum Theory
**Stationary orbits:** electrons revolve only in specific, fixed, non-radiating circular paths
**Energy quantization:** energy is only emitted or absorbed when an electron jumps from one orbit to another: ΔE = hν

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Practical Application
notes: Successfully calculates the exact radius of orbits, the velocity of electrons, and the energy of an electron for hydrogen-like (single-electron) species: H, He⁺, Li²⁺

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Defects
notes: Failed to predict the spectra of multi-electron atoms, such as Helium or Carbon
Could not explain the splitting of spectral lines under a magnetic field (**Zeeman Effect**) or an electric field (**Stark Effect**)

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Absorption vs Emission
notes: While an electron stays within a single stationary orbit, it neither gains nor loses energy
**Jumping up** to an outer (higher-energy) track = absorbing energy
**Dropping down** to an inner (lower-energy) track = releasing energy as a flash of light (a photon)

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Bohr's Atomic Model — Quantization of Angular Momentum
notes: The postulate that formally restricts which orbits are allowed: the electron's angular momentum is quantized in integer multiples of h/2π
**mvr = nh/2π**, where m = electron mass, v = electron velocity, r = orbit radius, n = 1, 2, 3... (the principal/orbit quantum number)

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: The Hydrogen Spectrum — Origin & Spectral Series
notes: When hydrogen gas is excited (e.g. electrically), electrons absorb energy and jump to higher tracks; when they fall back down to lower tracks, they release that exact energy as light of a specific wavelength
Because transitions happen only between specific fixed tracks, the emitted light forms discrete, sharp spectral lines rather than a continuous rainbow

Each spectral series corresponds to electrons landing on one specific base track (n₁): **Lyman** → n₁ = 1 (ultraviolet, invisible); **Balmer** → n₁ = 2 (the only series visible to the human eye, as coloured lines); **Paschen** → n₁ = 3 (infrared); **Brackett** → n₁ = 4 (infrared); **Pfund** → n₁ = 5 (far-infrared)

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: The Hydrogen Spectrum — Rydberg Equation
notes: 1/λ = R_H·(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), where λ = wavelength of emitted light, R_H = Rydberg constant, n₁ = lower (final) orbit, n₂ = higher (initial) orbit
The **series limit** (shortest wavelength, highest-energy line in a series) occurs as n₂ → ∞, giving the simplified form 1/λ = R_H/n₁²

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Negative Electronic Energy & the Bohr Mechanical Model Critique
notes: **Negative electronic energy:** the energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit is taken as negative because the electron is bound to the nucleus; energy must be supplied to remove it. The most negative energy corresponds to the most stable (lowest) orbit, n = 1.

**Bohr mechanical model critique:** Bohr treated the electron as a tiny planet moving in a definite circular orbit, a purely mechanical picture. It could not explain why only certain orbits were allowed, nor why the electron did not radiate while moving in a stationary orbit.

**Quantum mechanical shift:** the mechanical orbit picture was replaced by a probabilistic, wave-based description in which the electron's position is described by a wave function rather than a fixed path.

**Schrödinger (1926):** Erwin Schrödinger introduced a wave equation whose solutions (wave functions, ψ) describe the electron's behaviour in three dimensions, giving rise to the modern orbital concept.
**Matter wave introduction:** the idea that particles such as electrons also behave as waves (de Broglie) laid the foundation for the wave-mechanical model.
**Einstein relation:** the equivalence of mass and energy, E = mc², connects the particle and wave descriptions of matter.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: de Broglie Matter Waves & the Einstein–Planck Synthesis
notes: **Einstein–Planck synthesis:** combining Einstein's mass–energy equivalence E = mc² with Planck's quantum relation E = hν gives mc² = hν, linking a particle's mass to a wave frequency.
**de Broglie wavelength:** since ν = c/λ, the relation becomes mc = h/λ, so the wavelength of a moving particle is λ = h/(mv) = h/p, where p = mv is the momentum.
**Inverse mass dependence:** λ ∝ 1/m — heavier objects have extremely short wavelengths, which is why macroscopic objects show no observable wave behaviour.
**Macro-object wave negligibility:** for everyday objects the de Broglie wavelength is far smaller than any measurable scale, so wave effects are undetectable and classical mechanics applies.

**Bohr quantization deduced via waves:** if an electron is a standing wave, only orbits whose circumference is an integer multiple of the wavelength (2πr = nλ) are stable — this naturally reproduces Bohr's quantization of angular momentum.

**Heisenberg (1927) introduction:** the wave picture of the electron led Heisenberg to the uncertainty principle, which states that position and momentum cannot both be known precisely at the same time.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle (1927)
notes: **Statement:** it is impossible to determine simultaneously and with unlimited precision both the exact position (x) and the exact momentum (p) of a sub-atomic particle such as an electron.
**Mathematical form:** Δx · Δp ≥ h / 4π, where Δx is the uncertainty in position, Δp is the uncertainty in momentum and h = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s is Planck's constant.
**Momentum form:** since Δp = m · Δv, the principle can be written as Δx · Δv ≥ h / (4πm) — for a heavy particle (large m) the product of uncertainties is tiny, so classical certainty is recovered.

**Wavelength measurement intrusion paradox:** observing an electron requires hitting it with photons; a shorter-wavelength photon gives better position information but delivers a larger kick that disturbs the electron's momentum, and vice versa — the act of measurement inevitably perturbs the system.
**Certainty / uncertainty complementarity:** precise knowledge of position destroys knowledge of momentum; the two are complementary and cannot be measured sharply at the same time.
**Probability space concept:** because the electron cannot be pinned to a definite point, its location is described by a probability distribution rather than a fixed path.

**Bohr definite-orbit fallacy:** a precise orbit would require exactly known position and momentum simultaneously, which the uncertainty principle forbids — so Bohr's definite circular orbits are physically impossible.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Schrödinger's Wave Equation & the Orbit→Orbital Shift
notes: **3D wave equation (1926):** Schrödinger extended de Broglie's idea to three dimensions. For a particle of mass m moving with total energy E and potential energy V, the wave function ψ satisfies (∂²ψ/∂x²) + (∂²ψ/∂y²) + (∂²ψ/∂z²) + (8π²m/h²)(E − V)ψ = 0.

**Wave function interpretation:** ψ itself has no direct physical meaning, but ψ² gives the probability of finding the electron in a small volume around a point — the electron cloud picture replaces the fixed orbit.

**Orbit → orbital paradigm shift:** an orbit is a definite circular path (Bohr), while an orbital is a three-dimensional region of space where the probability of finding the electron is high (usually taken as ~90–95%).

**Quantum numbers emerge naturally:** solving the equation for the hydrogen atom yields three integer quantum numbers (n, l, m) that characterise each allowed orbital, with a fourth (s) added later for spin.
**Subshell subdivision (s, p, d, f):** orbitals of the same principal shell are grouped into subshells labelled s, p, d and f, which differ in shape, energy and orientation.
**Spherical vs directional geometry:** s-orbitals are spherical, while p-orbitals are dumb-bell shaped and directional along the x, y and z axes; d and f orbitals have more complex shapes.
**Electron cloud mapping:** plotting ψ² in three dimensions gives the spatial probability maps (clouds) that replace Bohr's planar circular orbits.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Bohr–Bury Scheme (1921) — Subshell & Shell Capacity Rules
notes: **Bohr–Bury scheme (1921):** a set of rules for filling electrons into shells and subshells; electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels first (aufbau principle), so the order of filling runs 1s → 2s → 2p → 3s → 3p → 4s → 3d → 4p → 5s → 4d → 5p → 6s → 4f → 5d → 6p → 7s → 5f → 6d → 7p.
**Maximum shell capacity:** the maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n² — K: 2, L: 8, M: 18, N: 32.
**Subshell electron capacity:** s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10, f holds 14 electrons.
**Spatial configurations:** each subshell contains a fixed set of orbitals — s: 1, p: 3, d: 5, f: 7 — so a shell of principal quantum number n contains a total of n² orbitals.
**Valence shell limit:** the outermost (valence) shell can hold at most 8 electrons.
**Penultimate shell limit:** the second-outermost (penultimate) shell can hold at most 18 electrons; the third-outermost (antepenultimate) shell at most 32.
**Concentric capacity rings:** the electrons are distributed in concentric shells (K, L, M, N, …) around the nucleus, each ring accommodating its characteristic maximum.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Orbit vs Orbital — 10-Point Delta Table & the s-Orbital
notes: **Orbit vs orbital (10-point delta):** (1) an orbit is a definite circular path; an orbital is a region of high probability. (2) Orbits are planar; orbitals are three-dimensional. (3) Orbits come from Bohr's model; orbitals from quantum mechanics. (4) An orbit has a fixed radius; an orbital has no sharp boundary. (5) Orbits are described by one quantum number (n); orbitals by three (n, l, m). (6) Orbits imply exact position and momentum; orbitals obey the uncertainty principle. (7) Orbits can hold at most 2n² electrons; orbitals hold at most 2 electrons. (8) Orbits are circular; orbitals have varied shapes (spherical, dumb-bell, etc.). (9) Orbits are not observable; orbitals are mapped by probability density ψ². (10) Orbits were abandoned; orbitals are the accepted modern description.

**Electronic arrays:** the electron configurations of representative atoms follow the Bohr–Bury order — N (Z=7): 1s² 2s² 2p³; O (Z=8): 1s² 2s² 2p⁴; Ne (Z=10): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶; Mg (Z=12): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s²; Cl (Z=17): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵.

**s-orbital sharp metrics:** the s-orbital is spherical, non-directional, has no nodal plane, and its probability density is highest at the nucleus; it is the only orbital with a non-zero value at the nucleus.
**Opposite spins cancellation:** two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins (+½ and −½); their magnetic moments cancel, so a fully paired orbital contributes no net magnetism.
**Energy trend:** for a given principal shell the s-subshell lies lowest in energy: 1s < 2s < 3s < 4s < …

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: p-Orbital Geometry & the Four Quantum Numbers
notes: **p-orbital dumb-bell axes:** each p-orbital is dumb-bell (figure-of-eight) shaped with two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus, oriented along one of the three cartesian axes — pₓ, pᵧ and p_z — which are mutually perpendicular.
**Nodal plane zero points:** every p-orbital has a nodal plane through the nucleus where the probability of finding the electron is zero; for pₓ the nodal plane is the yz-plane, and so on.
**Degenerate energy states:** in a given shell all three p-orbitals have the same energy (they are degenerate); in the absence of a magnetic field they are indistinguishable energetically.

**Complex d/f shapes:** d-orbitals (l = 2) mostly have four-lobed cloverleaf shapes (with one two-lobed d_z² orbital plus a torus), while f-orbitals (l = 3) have even more complex multi-lobed geometries.

**Four quantum numbers categorical taxonomy:** every electron is uniquely specified by (1) the principal quantum number n (main energy level/shell), (2) the azimuthal quantum number l (subshell/shape), (3) the magnetic quantum number m (orbital orientation), and (4) the spin quantum number s (+½ or −½, direction of spin).
**Subshell maximum capacities:** s holds 2 electrons, p holds 6, d holds 10, f holds 14.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Quantum Number Origins — Principal, Azimuthal & Subshell Metrics
notes: **Schrödinger/Spin origins breakdown:** the principal (n), azimuthal (l) and magnetic (m) quantum numbers arise naturally as the three quantum conditions of Schrödinger's wave equation; the spin quantum number (s) was added later from the Stern–Gerlach and Goudsmit–Uhlenbeck experiments.
**Principal quantum number (n):** fixes the main energy level and size of the orbital (shell). n = 1, 2, 3, …; larger n means a larger, higher-energy orbital farther from the nucleus.

**Sommerfeld hyperfine line expansions:** Arnold Sommerfeld introduced the azimuthal (orbital) quantum number l to explain the hyperfine splitting of spectral lines observed under high resolution, which Bohr's model could not explain.
**Subsidiary (azimuthal) quantum number (l):** fixes the subshell and shape of the orbital; l takes integer values 0 to n − 1 and is labelled by letters — s: 0, p: 1, d: 2, f: 3.
**Subshell orbital count:** each subshell contains 2l + 1 orbitals — for s (l=0): 1, p (l=1): 3, d (l=2): 5, f (l=3): 7.
**Subshell electron count:** each subshell holds a maximum of 2(2l + 1) electrons — for s: 2, p: 6, d: 10, f: 14.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Orbital Designation Matrix — Magnetic & Spin Quantum Numbers
notes: **Tabular orbital designation matrix:** the complete set of orbitals for a given shell is catalogued by combining n, l and m. For n = 2: l = 0 gives the single 2s orbital (m = 0); l = 1 gives the three 2p orbitals (m = +1, 0, −1), designated 2pₓ, 2pᵧ, 2p_z.
**Magnetic quantum number (m):** fixes the orientation of the orbital in space relative to an applied magnetic field; m takes 2l + 1 integer values from −l to +l.
**m value sets by subshell:** for l = 0: m = 0 (1 orbital); l = 1: m = +1, 0, −1 (3 orbitals); l = 2: m = +2, +1, 0, −1, −2 (5 orbitals); l = 3: m = +3, +2, +1, 0, −1, −2, −3 (7 orbitals).
**Total orbitals in a shell:** a shell of principal quantum number n contains exactly n² orbitals, combining all subshells of that shell.

**Landé–Zeeman magnetic orientations:** in an external magnetic field, the degenerate orbitals of a subshell split into distinct energy levels (Zeeman effect), each orbital having a different spatial orientation — one line splits into 2l + 1 components.
**Goudsmit–Uhlenbeck electron axial rotation:** Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck proposed that the electron itself spins about its own axis, producing an intrinsic angular momentum and a tiny magnetic dipole.
**Clockwise vs anticlockwise spins:** the electron's spin can be clockwise or anticlockwise, giving two spin states; the spin quantum number s takes only two values: +½ and −½.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Electron Spin Notation (↑ ↓) & Shell Mapping Matrices
notes: **Arrowhead vector notation:** electrons are drawn as arrowheads — an upward arrow (↑) represents spin +½ (clockwise) and a downward arrow (↓) represents spin −½ (anticlockwise); each box (orbital) can hold at most two arrows of opposite direction.

**Net zero paired magnetic field cancellation:** when an orbital contains two electrons with opposite spins, their magnetic moments are equal and opposite, so the net magnetic field of the pair is zero — the atom as a whole becomes diamagnetic for that pair.

**K shell complete mapping matrix:** the K shell (n = 1) contains only the single 1s orbital; it is filled as 1s¹ (one ↑) for hydrogen and 1s² (↑↓) for helium, where the pair is fully spin-compensated.

**L shell complete mapping matrix:** the L shell (n = 2) contains the 2s orbital plus three 2p orbitals (2pₓ, 2pᵧ, 2p_z). Filling follows Hund's rule — electrons first occupy each orbital singly with parallel spins before pairing: e.g. oxygen (1s² 2s² 2p⁴) shows one paired 2p box (↑↓) and two half-filled boxes (↑, ↑).

**Arrow direction convention:** in electron configuration notation the order of filling is drawn left-to-right across the orbitals of the subshell, and the last electron added determines the arrow direction for half-filled orbitals.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: The Atom & Dalton's Atomic Theory
notes: **The composition of matter** was studied in the 18th century by different scientists.

**Atom definition:** all matter is made of millions of tiny particles called atoms. The word 'atom' comes from the Greek (a = absence, tomos = cut), meaning indivisible or indestructible — atoms are the smallest units of matter.
**Dalton's atomic theory (1808):** the concept of the atom was first put forward by the English chemist John Dalton, and his theory laid the foundation of modern atomic theory.
**Discovery of subatomic particles:** towards the end of the 19th century it became known that the atom consists of still smaller particles such as electrons, protons and neutrons.
**Further subatomic particles:** subsequent studies led to the discovery of meson, quark, gluon, neutrino, and antiparticles like positron, antiproton, antineutron etc.

**Fundamental particles:** the small particles present in an atom are called subatomic particles; more than 30 have been discovered. Electron, proton and neutron are the principal subatomic particles, generally referred to as fundamental particles.
Example subatomic particles: electrons, protons, neutrons, a positron (e⁺), meson, neutrino (π±), quark.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: The Electron — Discovery & Properties of Cathode Rays
notes: **Electron definition:** an electron is a negatively charged subatomic particle denoted with the symbol e⁻.
**Discovery (1897):** the electron was first discovered by Joseph John Thomson as a result of a discharge tube experiment.

**Discharge tube experiment:** Thomson filled gas in a specially designed glass tube provided with metal electrodes and passed high voltage electricity at low pressure (10,000 Volts at 10⁻² mmHg) through the tube.
**Cathode rays:** as a result, some rays started to flow from the cathode towards the anode, which are called cathode rays.
**Naming:** the term electron was given by George Johnstone Stoney (in 1891).

**Properties of cathode rays:** (a) they cast a shadow of an object on their way; (b) they travel in a straight line; (c) they are deflected towards the anode of the applied electric field, indicating they carry a negative charge; (d) they produce a heating effect when struck to a thin metal coil; (e) they can penetrate a thin sheet of metals; (f) they cause fluorescence on a zinc sulphide screen; (g) they ionize the gas through which they pass.
**Conclusion:** the observation of the above properties led to the conclusion that cathode rays carry a negative charge with a certain mass.
**Naming as electrons:** J.J. Thomson named cathode rays as electrons, symbolized with e⁻ or as a beta particle.
**Charge and mass:** the charge on an electron is -1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs and the mass is 9.1 × 10⁻²⁸ g, which is equal to 1/1837th of the mass of a hydrogen atom.
**e/m determination:** J.J. Thomson determined the e/m (specific charge) value of the electron and Millikan determined the charge of the electron.
**e/m order:** the increasing order of the value of e/m is neutron < alpha-ray < proton < electron.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: The Proton — Discovery & Properties of Anode Rays
notes: **Proton definition:** a proton is a positively charged subatomic particle denoted with the symbol p⁺.

**Context of discovery:** it was discovered after the discovery of electrons, with the assumption that positive particles must also exist alongside negative particles since an atom is electrically neutral.
**Discovery (1886):** the proton was discovered by Eugen Goldstein by a discharge tube experiment like that for electrons.
**Experiment:** he passed high voltage electricity through a discharge tube filled with hydrogen gas and provided with a perforated metal cathode.
**Chemical equation:** H → H⁺ + e⁻ (proton formation).
**Low pressure:** the discharge was carried out at low pressure.
**Canal rays:** he observed rays travelling opposite to the cathode rays; these were deflected towards the cathode of the applied field and thus called anode rays, positive rays, or canal rays.

**Properties of anode rays:** (a) they cast a shadow of the objects in their path; (b) they travel in a straight line; (c) they are deflected towards the cathode of the applied electric or magnetic field; (d) they cause a heating effect on metal coils; (e) they rotate a small paddle wheel placed on their path.
**Conclusion:** these properties led to the conclusion that anode rays carry a positive charge and possess a certain mass.
**Naming:** these rays were named protons by Goldstein and symbolized with p⁺.
**Charge:** the proton possesses +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulomb of electric charge, equal but opposite in sign to that of an electron.
**Mass:** a proton is much heavier than an electron; its mass is 1.672 × 10⁻²⁴ g, equal to the mass of the hydrogen atom.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: The Neutron — Discovery & Fundamental Particle Characteristics
notes: **Context of discovery:** the discovery of electrons and protons was followed by neutrons; the presence of a third type of sub-atomic particle is justified by the fact that atomic mass is not equal to the total mass of the protons present in an atom — it is much higher, as the mass of the electron is negligible.
**Discovery (1932):** this problem was solved by Sir James Chadwick by discovering the presence of neutral particles in an atom.
**Experiment:** he bombarded α-particles on a thin sheet of Beryllium and observed the emission of highly penetrating particles which were neutral.
**Naming:** Chadwick named the neutral particles neutrons.
**Mass:** neutrons possess a mass of 1.675 × 10⁻²⁴ g, which is slightly greater than that of protons.
**Nuclear reaction:** the nuclear reaction used to produce neutrons between α-ray and Beryllium is: ₂He⁴ + ₄Be⁹ → ₆C¹² + ₀n¹ (neutron).

**Fundamental particle summary:** atoms possess mainly three fundamental sub-atomic particles — electrons, protons, and neutrons. The protons and neutrons are present in the nucleus of an atom and are called nucleons; the electrons revolve around the nucleus in different orbits or shells.

**Characteristics table:** Electron (e⁻): mass 9.1 × 10⁻²⁸ g (0.00055 amu), charge -1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (-4.803 × 10⁻¹⁰ esu), discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897. Proton (p⁺): mass 1.672 × 10⁻²⁴ g (1.00732 amu), charge +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (+4.803 × 10⁻¹⁰ esu), discovered by E. Goldstein in 1886. Neutron (n⁰): mass 1.675 × 10⁻²⁴ g (1.00871 amu), charge 0, discovered by James Chadwick in 1932.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Atomic Number (Z)
notes: **Definition:** the number of unit positive charges carried by the nucleus of a neutral atom is known as the atomic number; in other words, the number of protons present in the nucleus of an atom is called the atomic number.

**Neutrality:** an atom is neutral due to the presence of an equal number of positive charges of protons and negative charges of electrons, so the atomic number can be considered as the number of electrons present in a neutral atom.
**Symbol:** the atomic number is generally denoted with the letter Z.
**Origin:** the concept of atomic number was first given by the scientist Moseley in 1913; Moseley formulated the modern periodic table based on increasing atomic numbers.
**Formulas:** Atomic number (Z) = number of protons (p⁺); Number of protons (p⁺) = number of electrons (e⁻) in a neutral atom; Z = p⁺ = e⁻.

**Example:** the atomic number of magnesium is 12, indicating there are 12 protons and 12 electrons in the atom. But the magnesium ion (Mg²⁺) possesses 12 protons and 10 electrons, and its atomic number is 12 and not 10.
**Notation:** in general, the atomic number of an element is written on the left side of the symbol of the element as a subscript.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Mass Number (A) & Isotopes
notes: **Mass number:** the sum of masses of sub-atomic particles contained in an atom is responsible for the mass of that atom. Since the mass of electrons is negligible, the mass of an atom is the sum of the masses of protons and neutrons present in the nucleus; the mass of an atom is concentrated on the nucleus.
**Whole number:** a mass number is a whole number since the number of protons and neutrons are whole numbers; it is generally denoted with the letter A.

**Notation:** the mass number is written as a superscript to the symbol of the element; for an atom (X) whose atomic number is Z and mass number is A, the symbol is written with Z as a subscript and A as a superscript.
**Formulas:** Mass number (A) = atomic number (Z) + number of neutrons (N); A = Z + N; A = p⁺ + n⁰; Mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons.
**Example:** ₁₂Mg²⁴ means the mass number of Mg is 24 amu, i.e., 12 protons and 12 neutrons.

**Isotopes definition:** in 1919, F.W. Aston found that certain elements consist of two or more types of atoms with the same atomic number but different mass numbers, which are called isotopes. The word isotope (coined by Soddy in 1913) comes from two Latin words, isos = the same and topos = position/place.

**Isotope properties:** isotopes are different atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different atomic masses; they possess the same position in the modern periodic table, have the same number of protons and electrons but a different number of neutrons, and possess identical chemical properties (due to same atomic number) but different physical properties (due to different mass numbers).

**Abundance:** around 1000 isotopes have been identified, of which nearly 300 are stable and occur in nature; the stability and natural abundance of isotopes differ. Chlorine has two isotopes, whereas krypton has nearly 20 isotopes. Most abundant isotopes occur from 90-99% with respect to other isotopes, but Cl-35 occurs 75% compared to Cl-37 (25%) in nature.

**Hydrogen isotopes:** hydrogen exists in three isotopic forms — protium (₁H¹), deuterium (₁H²), and tritium (₁H³), denoted with symbols H, D, and T respectively. Out of these, tritium is radioactive. Protium has no neutron, deuterium has one, and tritium has two. Natural abundance: protium 99.98%, deuterium about 0.015%, tritium only 10⁻¹⁵ %.

**Examples:** carbon isotopes ₆C¹², ₆C¹³, ₆C¹⁴ (most abundant ₆C¹²); nitrogen ₇N¹⁴, ₇N¹⁵ (₇N¹⁴); oxygen ₈O¹⁶, ₈O¹⁷, ₈O¹⁸ (₈O¹⁶); neon ₁₀Ne²⁰, ₁₀Ne²¹, ₁₀Ne²² (₁₀Ne²⁰); sulphur ₁₆S³², ₁₆S³³, ₁₆S³⁴, ₁₆S³⁶ (₁₆S³²); chlorine ₁₇Cl³⁵, ₁₇Cl³⁷ (₁₇Cl³⁵); uranium ₉₂U²³³, ₉₂U²³⁵, ₉₂U²³⁸ (₉₂U²³⁸).

**Isotopic effect:** the compounds formed by different isotopes possess different physical and chemical properties due to differences in the mass of the isotopes; this difference is called an isotopic effect. e.g. protium and deuterium separately combine with oxygen to give H₂O and D₂O respectively, whose boiling points, melting points, densities, and ionization constants differ to some extent.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Isobars, Isotones & Isodiaphers
notes: **Isobars:** several atoms having the same mass number but different atomic numbers are called isobars. The word 'isobar' derives from two Greek words, isos = equal and baros = heavy.

**Isobar properties:** isobars are atoms of different elements having different atomic numbers but the same mass number; they possess entirely different physical and chemical properties. The total number of nucleons (protons + neutrons) remains the same, while the number of protons and electrons differs.

**Isobar examples:** ₁₈Ar⁴⁰, ₁₉K⁴⁰, and ₂₀Ca⁴⁰ are isobars (same mass number 40); also ₆C¹⁴ and ₇N¹⁴ are isobars. Other examples: (i) ₃₂Ge⁷⁶, ₃₄Se⁷⁶; (ii) ₅₂Te¹³⁰, ₅₄Xe¹³⁰, ₅₆Ba¹³⁰; (iii) ₈₂Pb²¹⁴, ₈₃Bi²¹⁴, ₈₄Po²¹⁴; (iv) ₉₂U²³⁹, ₉₃Np²³⁹, ₉₄Pu²³⁹.

**Isotones:** different atoms having different atomic numbers and mass numbers but the same number of neutrons are called isotones. The word 'isotone' derives from Greek, isos = the same and tonos = neutrons.
**Isotone properties:** isotones have different physical and chemical properties since they are entirely different elements; the number of electrons and protons differ in isotones.
**Isotone examples:** ₆C¹⁴, ₇N¹⁵, and ₈O¹⁶ are isotones because each has the same number of neutrons (8).
**Isodiaphers:** several atoms having the same isotopic number or isotopic excess (number of neutrons − number of protons) are called isodiaphers.
**Isodiapher examples:** ₁₉K³⁹ and ₉F¹⁹ are isodiaphers.
**Nuclear composition of isotones:** ₆C¹⁴ (atomic number 6, mass 14, e⁻ 6, p⁺ 6, n⁰ 8); ₇N¹⁵ (atomic number 7, mass 15, e⁻ 7, p⁺ 7, n⁰ 8); ₈O¹⁶ (atomic number 8, mass 16, e⁻ 8, p⁺ 8, n⁰ 8).

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Thomson's Plum Pudding (Watermelon) Model
notes: **Context:** before 1898, the specific location of electrons and protons within an atom remained completely unknown.
**Proposal (1898):** J.J. Thomson proposed a simple model conceptually known as the 'watermelon model' (also called the plum pudding model).
**Structure:** Thomson considered the atom to be a solid sphere of uniform positive charge, with negatively charged electrons embedded within this positive sphere like seeds inside a watermelon.
**Fate:** this model failed to explain many subsequent practical and theoretical findings and was soon discarded.

**Alpha particle tool:** around the same period, radioactive elements like radium were found to produce dipositive helium ions with a charge of 2+ and a mass of 4 amu; an alpha particle is denoted He²⁺ or ₂He⁴, formed by the nuclear equation [He − 2e⁻ → He²⁺].

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Q: State the observations and conclusions of Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment
notes: **Observation 1:** most α-particles passed straight through the gold foil undeflected → most of the atom's volume is empty space

**Observation 2:** a small fraction were deflected at large angles, and a very small fraction bounced almost straight back → these particles must have encountered something small, dense, and positively charged
**Conclusion:** the atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre, with electrons occupying the mostly empty space around it

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Q: Why does Rutherford's nuclear model fail to explain the stability of an atom?
notes: Maxwell's theory states that any accelerating charge radiates electromagnetic energy
An electron orbiting the nucleus is constantly changing direction, so it is constantly accelerating, and by Maxwell's theory it should continuously lose energy as radiation

Losing energy means the electron's orbital radius should shrink, causing it to spiral inward and collapse into the nucleus within a fraction of a second — but real atoms are stable, which Rutherford's model cannot account for

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Q: How exactly did Bohr's model resolve the stability crisis left unsolved by Rutherford?
notes: Bohr proposed that electrons can only exist in specific 'stationary' orbits where they do NOT radiate energy, regardless of their acceleration — this postulate directly overrides the classical prediction that orbiting charges must radiate
Energy changes only happen in discrete jumps between these fixed orbits (ΔE = hν), not continuously, so there's no mechanism for a gradual energy loss and inward spiral

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Q: Bohr's model works well for hydrogen but fails for helium — why does adding one more electron break the model?
notes: Bohr's postulates and resulting equations were derived by balancing the electrostatic attraction between a single electron and the nucleus against the centripetal force needed for circular motion — a clean two-body problem

With two or more electrons, electron–electron repulsion enters the picture, making it a multi-body problem that Bohr's simple circular-orbit model has no mechanism to account for — this is why it accurately predicts the spectra of H, He⁺, and Li²⁺ (all single-electron species) but not neutral He or heavier atoms

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Q: What do the Zeeman and Stark effects reveal about the limits of Bohr's model?
notes: **Zeeman Effect:** spectral lines split into multiple closely spaced lines when the atom is placed in a magnetic field
**Stark Effect:** spectral lines split when the atom is placed in an electric field

Bohr's model treats each orbit as having a single fixed energy, so it cannot explain why a magnetic or electric field would split a single spectral line into several — this splitting requires additional quantum numbers (like the magnetic quantum number) that only came with the more advanced quantum mechanical model of the atom

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Q: State the three main observations of Rutherford's gold foil experiment and their corresponding conclusions
notes: **Observation 1:** most α-particles passed straight through the foil undeflected → **Conclusion:** atoms are mostly empty space

**Observation 2:** a small fraction were deflected through small-to-moderate angles → **Conclusion:** there is a concentration of positive charge somewhere in the atom that repels the positively charged α-particles

**Observation 3:** a very small fraction (about 1 in 8000) bounced back at large angles, close to 180° → **Conclusion:** this positive charge, along with almost all of the atom's mass, is concentrated in an extremely small volume — the nucleus

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Q (worked example): Calculate the radius of the electron in the 2nd orbit of a Li²⁺ ion
notes: Bohr radius formula: r_n = (0.529 Å)·n²/Z, where n = orbit number and Z = atomic number
For Li²⁺: Z = 3, n = 2
**Answer: r₂ ≈ 0.705 Å**

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Q (worked example): Calculate the wavelength of the series limit of the Lyman series for hydrogen
notes: The series limit occurs as n₂ → ∞, so 1/λ = R_H(1/n₁² − 0) = R_H/n₁²
For the Lyman series, n₁ = 1: 1/λ = 1.097 × 10⁷ × 1 = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹
**Answer: λ ≈ 91.15 nm** — deep ultraviolet, consistent with the Lyman series being a UV series

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Q: Which hydrogen spectral series falls entirely within the visible region of light, and why is it the only one?
notes: The **Balmer series** (n₁ = 2) is the only series entirely visible to the human eye
Its emitted wavelengths (transitions from n₂ = 3, 4, 5... down to n₁ = 2) happen to fall in the roughly 400–700 nm range that human eyes detect

The Lyman series (n₁ = 1) is higher-energy and shorter-wavelength (ultraviolet), while Paschen, Brackett, and Pfund (n₁ = 3, 4, 5) are lower-energy and longer-wavelength (infrared) — both fall outside the visible window

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Self-Practice Checkpoint — Negative Energy & Bohr Critique (Page 108)
notes: **Q1. Why is the energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit taken as negative?** Because the electron is bound to the nucleus; energy must be supplied to remove it. The most negative energy corresponds to the most stable (lowest) orbit, n = 1.

**Q2. State two major defects of Bohr's atomic model.** (1) It could not explain why only certain orbits are allowed (quantization was assumed, not derived). (2) It could not explain the spectra of atoms with more than one electron (e.g. helium), nor the fine structure of spectral lines.

**Q3. What is the significance of E = mc² in the development of quantum mechanics?** It links mass and energy, and combined with Planck's E = hν it leads to the de Broglie relation λ = h/(mv), showing that matter has wave-like properties.

**Q4. How did Schrödinger's 1926 work shift the atomic model?** Schrödinger replaced Bohr's definite circular orbits with a wave equation whose solutions (wave functions ψ) describe the electron's behaviour in three dimensions, giving rise to the probabilistic orbital concept.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Self-Practice Checkpoint — Duality & Principle Deflections (Page 111)
notes: **Q1. Distinguish between an orbit and an orbital.** An orbit is a definite circular path of the electron (Bohr model), planar and described by one quantum number n. An orbital is a three-dimensional region of high probability of finding the electron (quantum mechanics), described by three quantum numbers (n, l, m) and obeying the uncertainty principle.

**Q2. What is the physical significance of the wave function ψ and of ψ²?** ψ itself has no direct physical meaning; ψ² gives the probability density of finding the electron in a small volume around a point, which is used to map the electron cloud.

**Q3. Why did the wave-mechanical model replace Bohr's definite orbits?** Because the uncertainty principle forbids knowing position and momentum simultaneously, a definite orbit is impossible; the electron must instead be described by a probability distribution (orbital).

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Self-Practice Checkpoint — Numerical Verifications & Degeneracy Mappings (Page 114)
notes: **Q1. How many orbitals are present in the subshell with l = 2? What is its maximum electron capacity?** Number of orbitals = 2l + 1 = 2(2) + 1 = 5. Maximum electron capacity = 2(2l + 1) = 10. So the d subshell has 5 orbitals and holds up to 10 electrons.

**Q2. Write the four quantum numbers that completely describe an electron in the 3p orbital.** Principal n = 3, azimuthal l = 1, magnetic m = −1, 0 or +1 (three possible values), spin s = +½ or −½. Any one of the six possible combinations (3 values of m × 2 spins) describes an electron in 3p.

**Q3. How many degenerate orbitals are there in a p subshell, and why are they called degenerate?** There are three (pₓ, pᵧ, p_z). They have the same energy (they are degenerate) in the absence of an applied magnetic field.

**Q4. For the d subshell, verify the degeneracy mapping.** With l = 2, m takes the values +2, +1, 0, −1, −2, giving 2l + 1 = 5 degenerate orbitals; each holds 2 electrons, so the d subshell accommodates 10 electrons in total.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Q (worked examples): de Broglie Wavelength & Uncertainty Principle
notes: **Q1. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving with a velocity of 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s.** Using λ = h/(mv) with h = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg and v = 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s: λ = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 6.6 × 10⁶) = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / 6.006 × 10⁻²⁴ ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

**Q2. Why is the wave nature of a moving cricket ball (mass ≈ 0.15 kg) not observable?** Using λ = h/(mv), for even a small ball travelling at 30 m/s the wavelength is λ = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (0.15 × 30) ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻³⁴ m — far smaller than the size of a nucleus and completely unobservable; the wavelength is negligible for macroscopic objects (λ ∝ 1/m).

**Q3. If the uncertainty in the position of an electron is 10⁻¹⁰ m, what is the minimum uncertainty in its velocity?** Using Δx · Δv ≥ h/(4πm): Δv = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / (4 × 3.14 × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 10⁻¹⁰) = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ / 1.143 × 10⁻³⁹ ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m/s.

**Q4. Explain why Bohr's definite orbits contradict the uncertainty principle.** A definite orbit requires both position and momentum to be exactly known at every instant, but Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π forbids simultaneous exact knowledge — so the electron cannot follow a sharply defined circular path.

class-11/chemistry/unit-3-atomic-structu.title: Q (worked examples): Atomic Number, Mass Number & Isotopes
notes: **Q1. For the atom ₁₂Mg²⁴, find the number of protons, electrons and neutrons.** Atomic number Z = 12, so protons = 12 and electrons = 12 (neutral atom). Mass number A = 24, so neutrons = A − Z = 24 − 12 = 12.

**Q2. The magnesium ion Mg²⁺ has atomic number 12. How many protons and electrons does it contain?** Protons = Z = 12 (unchanged). Since the ion has lost 2 electrons, electrons = 12 − 2 = 10. Its atomic number remains 12.

**Q3. Protium (₁H¹), deuterium (₁H²) and tritium (₁H³) are isotopes. How do they differ?** All three have the same atomic number Z = 1 (one proton and one electron) but different mass numbers. Protium has 0 neutrons, deuterium has 1 neutron, and tritium has 2 neutrons. Protium is most abundant (99.98%), deuterium about 0.015%, and tritium only 10⁻¹⁵ % (radioactive).
