class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/notes/01.title: Quick Revision — Vectors
notes: - **Scalar:** magnitude only (mass, speed, work). **Vector:** magnitude + direction (velocity, force, displacement).
- **Resultant (parallelogram law):** $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$; direction $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}$.
- **Triangle & polygon laws:** resultant closes the vector polygon — head-to-tail addition.
- **Resolution:** a vector $\vec{A}$ at angle $\theta$ to the x-axis has components $A_x = A\cos\theta$, $A_y = A\sin\theta$; $A = \sqrt{A_x^2+A_y^2}$, $\tan\theta = A_y/A_x$.
- **Unit vector:** $\hat{A} = \dfrac{\vec{A}}{A}$ (dimensionless, magnitude 1); $\vec{A} = A\hat{A}$.
- **Scalar (dot) product:** $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta = A_xB_x+A_yB_y+A_zB_z$ (commutative, result is scalar).
- **Vector (cross) product:** $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = AB\sin\theta \,\hat{n}$ (direction by right-hand rule; result is vector).
- **Component form:** $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = (A_yB_z-A_zB_y)\hat{i}+(A_zB_x-A_xB_z)\hat{j}+(A_xB_y-A_yB_x)\hat{k}$.
- **Perpendicular** iff $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}=0$; **parallel** iff $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=0$.
- **Applications:** finding force components, displacement in planes, work $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{s}$, torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}$.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/pyqs/01-.title: NEB-Style Questions — Vectors
notes:
Q1. (Derivation) State and prove the parallelogram law of vector addition.
Ans: If two vectors $\vec{P}$, $\vec{Q}$ are represented by adjacent sides of a parallelogram, the resultant is the diagonal. From the geometry (perpendicular dropped on the extension of P): $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$ and $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}$.

Q2. (Numerical) Two forces 3 N and 4 N act at a point with an angle of 90° between them. Find the resultant.
Ans: $R = \sqrt{3^2+4^2+2(3)(4)\cos90°} = \sqrt{9+16} = 5\,\text{N}$, direction $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(4/3)\approx53.1°$.

Q3. (Concept) State the conditions under which two vectors are (i) perpendicular (ii) parallel.
Ans: (i) $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}=0$; (ii) $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=0$.

Q4. (Resolution) Resolve $\vec{F} = 10\,\text{N}$ at 30° above the horizontal into its components, $\cos30° = 0.866$, $\sin30° = 0.5$.
Ans: $F_x = 10\cos30° = 8.66\,\text{N}$; $F_y = 10\sin30° = 5\,\text{N}$.

Q5. (Definition) Distinguish between scalar and vector quantities with examples.
Ans: Scalar has magnitude only (mass, speed, work, temperature); vector has magnitude and direction (velocity, force, displacement, momentum).

Q6. (Dot product) Two vectors $\vec{A}=3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}$. Find the angle between them.
Ans: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}=3+8=11$; $|\vec{A}|=5$, $|\vec{B}|=\sqrt{5}$; $\cos\theta = 11/(5√5) \approx 0.984$, so $\theta \approx 10.3°$.

Q7. (Cross product) Find $\hat{i}\times\hat{j}$ and $\hat{i}\times\hat{k}$.
Ans: $\hat{i}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k}$; $\hat{i}\times\hat{k} = -\hat{j}$ (right-hand rule).

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/sets/01-.title: Parallelogram Law — Worked Examples
notes: **Q1. Two equal vectors have a resultant equal in magnitude to either vector. Find the angle between them.** Let $P=Q=x$ and $R=x$. Then $x^2=x^2+x^2+2x^2\cos\theta \Rightarrow \cos\theta=-\tfrac12 \Rightarrow \theta=120°$.

**Q2. Two equal vectors are inclined at angle $\theta$ to each other. Show that the angle $\alpha$ between the resultant and each vector is $\theta/2$.** With $P=Q$: $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{Q+Q\cos\theta}=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta}$. Using half-angle identities $\sin\theta=2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)$ and $1+\cos\theta=2\cos^2(\theta/2)$, this simplifies to $\tan\alpha=\tan(\theta/2)$, so $\alpha=\theta/2$.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/sets/02-.title: Resolution of Vectors — Worked Examples
notes: **Q1. Two forces, 10 N acting at 30° above the +x-axis and 5 N acting at 45° below the +x-axis, act at a point. Find the resultant.** $F_x = 10\cos30° + 5\cos45° = 8.66+3.54=12.20\,\text{N}$. $F_y = 10\sin30° - 5\sin45° = 5-3.54=1.46\,\text{N}$ (the second force's y-component is negative since it is below the axis). $F=\sqrt{F_x^2+F_y^2}=\sqrt{12.20^2+1.46^2}\approx12.28\,\text{N}$, at $\theta=\tan^{-1}(1.46/12.20)\approx6.8°$ above the x-axis.

**Q2. Two forces, 10 N and 5 N, each act at 30° from a common reference line, one above it and one below it. Find the resultant.** $F_x = 10\cos30°+5\cos30° = (10+5)\times(\sqrt3/2)=7.5\sqrt3\approx12.99\,\text{N}$. $F_y = 10\sin30° - 5\sin30° = 5-2.5=2.5\,\text{N}$. $F=\sqrt{F_x^2+F_y^2}=\sqrt{12.99^2+2.5^2}\approx13.23\,\text{N}$, at $\theta=\tan^{-1}(2.5/12.99)\approx10.9°$ from the reference line, on the side of the larger (10 N) force.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/sets/03-.title: Dot Product — Worked Examples
notes: **Q1. Find $|\vec{A}|$, $|\vec{B}|$, $|\vec{A}+\vec{B}|$ and $|\vec{A}-\vec{B}|$ for $\vec{A}=5\hat{i}+4\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B}=4\hat{i}+6\hat{j}$.** $|\vec{A}|=\sqrt{5^2+4^2}=\sqrt{41}$. $|\vec{B}|=\sqrt{4^2+6^2}=\sqrt{16+36}=\sqrt{52}$. $\vec{A}+\vec{B}=9\hat{i}+10\hat{j} \Rightarrow |\vec{A}+\vec{B}|=\sqrt{81+100}=\sqrt{181}$. $\vec{A}-\vec{B}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j} \Rightarrow |\vec{A}-\vec{B}|=\sqrt{1+4}=\sqrt5$.

**Q2. Find the angle between $\vec{a}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$.** $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=2(2)+3(3)+4(-4)=4+9-16=-3$. $|\vec{a}|=|\vec{c}|=\sqrt{4+9+16}=\sqrt{29}$ (both vectors have the same magnitude here). $\cos\theta=\dfrac{-3}{29}\approx-0.103 \Rightarrow \theta\approx95.9°$ (obtuse, since the dot product is negative).

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/sets/04-.title: Finding the Resultant of Two Perpendicular Vectors of Equal Magnitude
notes: **If two vectors of equal magnitude act perpendicular to each other, find the resultant.** Let $|\vec{A}|=|\vec{B}|=a$ and $\theta=90°$. Using $R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}=\sqrt{a^2+a^2+2a^2\cos90°}=\sqrt{2a^2}=a\sqrt2$. Direction: $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{a\sin90°}{a+a\cos90°}=\dfrac{a}{a}=1 \Rightarrow \alpha=45°$ — the resultant bisects the angle between the two equal perpendicular vectors.

**Q. If two equal vectors act perpendicular to each other and their resultant is 1.414 ($\approx\sqrt2$) units, find the magnitude of each vector.** Using $R=a\sqrt2$ from above: $a=\dfrac{R}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}=1$ unit — each vector has magnitude 1 unit.

class-11/physics/unit-2-vectors/sets/05-.title: Two Vectors, North-of-East / South-of-East Example (Perpendicular Resultant)
notes: **If two vectors of equal magnitude 2 m act perpendicular to each other, find the resultant.** Let $|\vec{A}|=|\vec{B}|=2\,\text{m}$, $\theta=90°$: $R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}=\sqrt{2^2+2^2+0}=\sqrt8=2\sqrt2\,\text{m}$.

Direction: $\tan\alpha=B/A=1 \Rightarrow \alpha=45°$, i.e. the resultant lies exactly midway between the two original vectors (e.g. if one points north-of-east and the other south-of-east, the resultant points due east).

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/conce.title: Motion, Frames of Reference & Branches of Mechanics
notes: **Mechanics** is the branch of physics that deals with bodies at rest (statics), in motion (kinematics) and the forces causing that motion (dynamics). It is the foundation on which the whole of physics is built.

**What mechanics answers:** *If I know an object's position, velocity and acceleration, can I predict where it will be in the future?* For everyday speeds, classical mechanics (Newtonian) gives accurate answers; near the speed of light relativity replaces it, and at atomic scales quantum mechanics takes over.
**Branches of mechanics:**
- **Statics** — bodies at rest; conditions of equilibrium (resultant force = 0, resultant torque = 0).
- **Kinematics** — describes *how* things move (position, velocity, acceleration) without asking why; the geometry of motion.
- **Dynamics** — relates *why* things move as they do: the study of forces (Newton's laws) and their effect on motion.

**Particle (point object):** a body whose size and shape are negligible compared to the distances involved (e.g. a cricket ball compared to a football field). Its whole mass is assumed concentrated at a point.

**Frame of reference:** a coordinate system (origin + axes + clock) fixed to an observer. A correct description of motion requires a stated frame — an apple 'at rest' in the train is moving at 120 km/h in the station frame.

**Distance vs displacement:** distance is the total path length travelled (scalar, ≥ 0); displacement is the change in position — the straight line from initial to final point (vector, depends only on endpoints).
**Speed vs velocity:** speed = distance/time (scalar); velocity = displacement/time (vector, includes direction). Average velocity over a round trip is zero even though average speed is not.

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/conce.title: Instantaneous Velocity & Instantaneous Acceleration
notes: **Instantaneous velocity** is the velocity of a body at a particular instant of time: v = lim(Δt→0) Δx/Δt = dx/dt. Geometrically it is the **slope of the position–time graph** at that instant.
**Instantaneous acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity at an instant: a = lim(Δt→0) Δv/Δt = dv/dt = d²x/dt². Geometrically it is the **slope of the velocity–time graph**.
**Uniform motion:** when velocity is constant, acceleration is zero and the x–t graph is a straight line.
**Uniformly accelerated motion:** acceleration is constant; the v–t graph is a straight line whose slope equals the acceleration.

**Sign convention:** choose a positive direction once; quantities along it are positive, opposite to it are negative. A body thrown upward has positive velocity but negative acceleration (g acts downward) — so it slows, stops momentarily (v = 0 at top), then falls back.
**Slopes on graphs:**
- x–t graph slope → velocity; straightening means uniform velocity, curving means acceleration.
- v–t graph slope → acceleration; area under the graph → displacement (distance when speed is constant sign).

**From a v–t graph:** area between the curve and the time axis in intervals where v > 0 is positive displacement, where v < 0 is negative displacement; total path length needs the areas added with magnitude.

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/conce.title: Relative Velocity
notes: **Relative velocity** of body A with respect to body B, written v_AB, is the velocity A appears to have when viewed from B's frame: v_AB = v_A − v_B (vectors measured in the same frame).
**Same direction:** if A and B move along the same line with speeds v_A and v_B, (i) chasing in the same direction → v_AB = v_A − v_B; (ii) moving towards each other → v_AB = v_A + v_B.
**Perpendicular tracks:** magnitude is found by the vector triangle, |v_AB| = √(v_A² + v_B²), directed according to the closing side of the triangle.
**Two practical results:**
- Time to meet/close a gap = (relative distance)/(relative speed).
- A person who appears to be running due north on a train moving east is actually moving northeast in the ground frame — always state the frame before quoting a velocity.

**Rain–umbrella problem:** a rain falling vertically with speed v_R appears slanted to a runner moving horizontally at v_M; the umbrella must be tilted by θ = tan⁻¹(v_M/v_R) from the vertical to cancel the horizontal component.

**River–boat (crossing) problem:** the resultant velocity of a boat steering across a flowing river is the vector sum of its velocity in still water and the river's velocity; to cross the river in a straight line perpendicular to the banks the boat must be steered inclined upstream.
**When v_AB = 0** the two bodies have the same velocity (no relative motion) — this is why two cars driving at equal speeds on a highway appear stationary to each other.

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/conce.title: Equations of Motion (Graphical Derivation)
notes: For a body moving with **uniform acceleration a** starting with initial velocity u, the three equations of motion are:
**1. v = u + at** — from the slope of the v–t graph: acceleration a = (v − u)/t.
**2. s = ut + ½at²** — from the area under the v–t graph (rectangle ut + triangle ½·t·at).
**3. v² = u² + 2as** — eliminating t between the first two equations.
**Graphical meaning (v–t graph):**
- The graph is a straight line of slope a.
- Intercept on the velocity axis = u.
- Area under the line between t = 0 and t = t = displacement s.
**Vector convention:** u, v, a, s are signed; choose up (or the initial direction) as positive. Falling bodies are handled with u = 0, a = +g downward.
**Special cases:**
- u = 0 (start from rest): v = at; s = ½at²; v² = 2as.
- Body finally at rest (v = 0): braking problems use v² = u² − 2as to find stopping distance.
- At t = 0 the equations reduce to the initial state — always check the sign of s when the body reverses direction (e.g. up and down motion).

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/conce.title: Motion of a Freely Falling Body
notes: **Free fall:** the motion of a body under the influence of gravity alone, with no air resistance. All bodies — heavy or light — fall with the same acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (Galileo's principle; independent of mass).
**Acceleration due to gravity g** is directed vertically downward; conventionally taken positive downward.
**Equations for free fall from rest (taking downward as positive):**
- v = gt
- h = ½gt²
- v² = 2gh
**Thrown vertically upward with speed u (taking upward as positive, g negative):**
- Time to reach the highest point: t = u/g (since v = 0 at top).
- Maximum height: H = u²/(2g).
- Total time of flight: T = 2u/g — the return journey takes exactly as long as the ascent.
- Speed on return to the launch point = u (velocity is −u).
**Key exam points:**
- At the highest point velocity is zero but acceleration is still g (never zero).
- Time of ascent = time of descent (for equal heights, same g).
- In the first second a body dropped from rest falls 4.9 m; distances in successive seconds are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 … (odd numbers) for uniform acceleration from rest.

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/conce.title: Projectile Motion & Its Applications
notes: **Projectile:** a body given an initial velocity and then allowed to move under gravity alone (air resistance neglected). Examples: a cricket ball, a javelin, water from a hose.
**Independent components:** resolve the initial velocity u at angle θ with the horizontal into uₓ = u cosθ (constant, because no horizontal force) and u_y = u sinθ (changes under g).
**Key results (derived from the two independent motions):**
- Horizontal velocity is constant: vₓ = u cosθ.
- Vertical motion is uniform acceleration: v_y = u sinθ − gt.
- Time of flight: T = 2u sinθ / g.
- Maximum height: H = u² sin²θ / (2g).
- Horizontal range: R = u² sin2θ / g.
**Range is maximum at θ = 45°:** R_max = u²/g (since sin2θ = 1). For every other range value there are two complementary angles θ and (90° − θ) that give the same range.
**Trajectory is a parabola:** y = x tanθ − (g x²)/(2 u² cos²θ) — a quadratic in x.
**Applications:**
- Sports (javelin/shot-put thrown at ~45°), ballistics, fire hoses, and understanding why a projectile fired horizontally and one dropped from the same height hit the ground at the same time.
- For a body projected horizontally (θ = 0) from height h: time to fall t = √(2h/g), horizontal range x = u√(2h/g).
**Common exam trap:** at the top of the trajectory the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity u cosθ is not — the projectile never stops.

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/formu.title: Key Equations — Kinematics
notes: - **v = u + at** (velocity after time t)
- **s = ut + ½at²** (displacement after time t)
- **v² = u² + 2as** (velocity–displacement relation)
- **v = dx/dt** (instantaneous velocity), **a = dv/dt** (instantaneous acceleration)
- **Relative velocity:** v_AB = v_A − v_B
- **Free fall (from rest):** v = gt, h = ½gt², v² = 2gh
- **Vertical throw up:** t = u/g to top, H = u²/(2g), T = 2u/g
- **Projectile:** T = 2u sinθ/g, H = u² sin²θ/(2g), R = u² sin2θ/g
- **Max range:** R_max = u²/g at θ = 45°
- **Trajectory equation:** y = x tanθ − g x²/(2u² cos²θ) — a parabola

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/pyqs/.title: NEB-Style Questions — Kinematics
notes:
Q1. (Short answer) Define instantaneous velocity and instantaneous acceleration. How are they obtained graphically?
Ans: v = dx/dt (slope of x–t curve); a = dv/dt (slope of v–t curve).

Q2. (Short answer) A ball is projected horizontally from a height h with speed u. Find the time to hit the ground and the horizontal range.
Ans: t = √(2h/g); range = u√(2h/g).

Q3. (Derivation) Derive s = ut + ½at² by velocity–time graph.
Ans: Area under v–t line = rectangle ut + triangle ½ t·(at) = ut + ½at².

Q4. (Numerical) A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s. Find acceleration and distance covered.
Ans: a = (v−u)/t = 2 m/s²; s = ut + ½at² = (0) + ½·2·100 = 100 m.

Q5. (Numerical) A stone is thrown vertically upward with velocity 30 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). Compute max height, time to reach the top and total time of flight.
Ans: H = u²/(2g) = 900/20 = 45 m; t_asc = u/g = 3 s; total T = 2u/g = 6 s.

Q6. (Concept) Two projectiles thrown at θ and 90° − θ with the same speed. Show they have equal ranges and derive the condition for maximum range.
Ans: R = u² sin2θ/g; sin2(90°−θ) = sin2θ so ranges equal; R is max when sin2θ = 1 → θ = 45°.

Q7. (Practical) Why is 45° the ideal angle for a long jump/javelin? 
Ans: Range R = u² sin2θ/g is greatest at 45° where sin2θ = 1; real athletes adjust for height of release and air drag.

class-11/physics/unit-3-kinematics/sets/.title: Practice Set 2 — Kinematics Short Questions
notes:
Q1. Distinguish between distance and displacement.
Answer: Distance is the total path length covered (scalar); displacement is the straight-line change of position (vector, direction included). Distance ≥ |displacement|.

Q2. Distinguish between speed and velocity.
Answer: Speed = distance/time (scalar, always positive); velocity = displacement/time (vector). Average velocity can be zero while average speed is not.

Q3. Can a body have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration? Give an example.
Answer: Yes. At the highest point of a vertically thrown ball, v = 0 but a = g (downward).

Q4. Define relative velocity. Write the relation for two bodies moving along the same straight line.
Answer: v_AB = v_A − v_B. Approaching each other: relative speed = v_A + v_B; chasing: = v_A − v_B.

Q5. Derive v² = u² + 2as graphically.
Answer: From the v–t graph of uniform acceleration, area under the line = s = average velocity × t = ((u+v)/2)t; with v = u + at, eliminating t gives v² = u² + 2as.

Q6. State the conditions for a projectile to have maximum range and equal ranges.
Answer: Range R = u² sin2θ/g is maximum at θ = 45°. Angles θ and (90° − θ) give the same range.

Q7. A stone is thrown vertically up and returns to the thrower's hand. Compare time of ascent and descent.
Answer: They are equal, because the upward and downward journeys have equal displacement (and equal speed magnitudes at every height).

class-11/physics/unit-4-dynamics/concept.title: Newton's Laws of Motion (Foundations of Dynamics)
notes: **Dynamics** is the branch of mechanics that relates the *motion* of bodies to the *forces* that cause it. Newton's three laws of motion are its foundation.

**First law (Law of Inertia):** a body at rest stays at rest, and a body in uniform straight-line motion stays in that motion, unless acted on by an external force. Inertia is the natural tendency of matter to resist changes in its state of motion.

**Second law (Law of Acceleration):** the net external force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration, F_net = ma = d(p)/dt. The direction of acceleration is the same as the direction of the net force.
**Mass as a measure of inertia:** the heavier (more massive) a body, the larger the force needed to produce a given acceleration — mass quantifies the inertia of a body.
**Third law (Action–Reaction):** for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; forces always occur in pairs — F_AB = −F_BA, acting on two *different* bodies (never cancel each other).
**Why action-reaction forces do not cancel:** the pair acts on different objects, so each body experiences only one of the two forces; the 'net force equals ma' applies to forces on a single body.
**Applications of Newton's laws:**
- Rocket propulsion (reaction of ejected gases pushes the rocket forward).
- a person walking pushes the ground backward; the ground pushes the person forward.
- A boat pushed back as a person steps off it (recoil).
**Units of force:** newton (N) = kg·m/s². 1 newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².

class-11/physics/unit-4-dynamics/concept.title: Linear Momentum, Impulse & Conservation of Linear Momentum
notes: **Linear momentum** p of a body is the product of its mass and velocity: p = mv. It is a vector pointing in the direction of motion; SI unit kg·m/s (also written N·s).
**Newton's second law in momentum form:** the net force equals the rate of change of momentum: F_net = dp/dt. For constant mass this reduces to F = ma.
**Impulse** is the product of force and the time for which it acts: J = F·Δt = Δp (change in momentum). Impulse is a vector, unit N·s = kg·m/s.
**Impulse–momentum theorem:** the impulse delivered to a body equals the total change in its momentum: J = F̄·Δt = p_final − p_initial = mv − mu.

**Why padding/crumple zones save lives:** in a collision the change of momentum is fixed, so extending the time Δt (airbags, crumple zones, long catches) reduces the average force F = Δp/Δt — a gentler stop.

**Conservation of linear momentum:** if the net external force on a system is zero, the total linear momentum of the system is constant (p_initial = p_final). Collisions and explosions conserve momentum because the internal action–reaction forces cancel.
**Recoil of a gun:** before firing, total momentum = 0; after firing, m_gun·v_gun + m_bullet·v_bullet = 0, so the gun recoils backward with momentum equal and opposite to the bullet.
**Applications:** rocket propulsion, jet engines, firing a cannon, and explaining why a person recoils when throwing a heavy object while standing on frictionless ice.

class-11/physics/unit-4-dynamics/concept.title: Moment, Torque & Conditions of Equilibrium
notes: **Moment of a force (torque)** about a point is the turning effect of the force: τ = F × r = magnitude F·d, where d is the perpendicular distance of the line of action from the pivot. Unit is N·m.
**Torque is a vector:** its direction is given by the right-hand rule (outward for anticlockwise, inward for clockwise about the axis).
**Conditions of equilibrium:**
- Translational (no net force): ΣF = 0 (a body at rest stays at rest; its centre of mass does not accelerate).
- Rotational (no net torque): Στ = 0 about any point.

**Moment of a couple:** two equal, opposite, parallel forces separated by distance d produce a couple with moment τ = F·d; a couple produces rotation with no net translation, and its moment is the same about every point.
**Balancing seesaw / lever problems** use Σ(clockwise moments) = Σ(anticlockwise moments) taken about the pivot, together with the weight acting at the centre of gravity.
**Centre of gravity** is the point where the total weight may be taken to act; for a uniform rod it is its midpoint — this is why a uniform plank balances about its centre.

**Practical examples:** a spanner turning a nut experiences greatest torque when the applied force is at the farthest end perpendicular to the handle; a door opens most easily when pushed at its edge, not near the hinge.

class-11/physics/unit-4-dynamics/concept.title: Solid Friction: Laws of Friction & Their Verification
notes: **Friction** is the force that opposes relative sliding (or the tendency to slide) between two surfaces in contact. It acts parallel to the surfaces, opposing the motion or the attempted motion.

**Static friction:** the force that prevents a body at rest from starting to move. It increases with the applied force up to a maximum value f_s,max = μ_s·N, where μ_s is the coefficient of static friction and N is the normal reaction.
**Limiting (maximum) static friction** is reached just before the body starts to move; beyond this, the body slides and kinetic (sliding) friction acts.
**Kinetic friction:** the opposing force once sliding occurs: f_k = μ_k·N, with μ_k typically slightly smaller than μ_s.
**Laws of solid friction (verified experimentally):**
1. Friction is independent of the area of contact (for the same normal force).
2. Friction is directly proportional to the normal reaction: f ∝ N, giving f = μN.
3. The force of friction depends on the nature of the two surfaces (roughness), characterised by μ.
4. Kinetic friction is independent of the relative speed of sliding (over ordinary ranges).

**Verification:** a block on a horizontal plank pulled by a spring balance shows the friction reading rising to a limiting value and then dropping slightly once sliding begins — demonstrating μ_s > μ_k.
**Friction can be useful or wasteful:** it enables walking, driving (tyres grip the road) and braking, but causes wear and energy loss in machines, which is why lubricants and ball bearings are used.

**Relation between μ and angle of friction/cone:** the angle of friction θ is given by tanθ = μ; it equals the angle of repose — the steepest angle at which a body just stays at rest on an inclined plane.

class-11/physics/unit-4-dynamics/formula.title: Key Equations — Dynamics
notes: - **Newton's second law:** F_net = ma = dp/dt
- **Linear momentum:** p = mv (kg·m/s)
- **Impulse:** J = F·Δt = Δp = mv − mu (N·s)
- **Conservation of momentum:** Σp before = Σp after
- **Static friction (max):** f_s = μ_s·N
- **Kinetic friction:** f_k = μ_k·N

- **Equilibrium:** ΣF = 0, Στ = 0
- **Recoil:** m_gun·v_gun + m_bullet·v_bullet = 0

- **Newton's third law:** F_AB = −F_BA, forces act on different bodies.

class-11/physics/unit-4-dynamics/pyqs/01.title: NEB-Style Questions — Dynamics
notes:
Q1. (Short answer) State Newton's first law and explain how mass measures inertia.
Ans: A body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force. Inertia is quantified by mass: for a fixed force, a = F/m, so larger m means smaller acceleration.

Q2. (Derivation) Prove the impulse–momentum theorem from Newton's second law.
Ans: F = ma = m(v − u)/t ⇒ F·t = m(v − u) = mv − mu = Δp = J.

Q3. (Numerical) A 1500-kg car moving at 20 m/s is stopped in 4 s by braking. Find the average braking force.
Ans: Δp = 1500(0 − 20) = −30000 kg·m/s; F = Δp/Δt = −30000/4 = −7500 N (magnitude 7500 N).

Q4. (Short answer) State conservation of linear momentum and give two applications.
Ans: Total momentum remains constant if no external net force. Applications: rocket propulsion and gun recoil.

Q5. (Derivation) Express the limiting friction in terms of the normal reaction and the coefficient of friction. Why is μ_s > μ_k?
Ans: f = μN; static friction must be overcome to start motion while kinetic friction sustains sliding — interlocking of surface irregularities is greater while at rest, so μ_s > μ_k.

Q6. (Numerical) A force of 50 N acts for 0.1 s on a 4 kg body at rest. Find impulse and the final velocity.
Ans: J = FΔt = 50 × 0.1 = 5 N·s; v = J/m = 5/4 = 1.25 m/s.

Q7. (Concept) Why do vehicles use brakes that increase friction on the road?
Ans: Friction between tyres and road provides the deceleration; more friction (better grip) gives the shorter stopping distance via F = ma.

class-11/physics/unit-4-dynamics/sets/01.title: Practice Set 1 — Dynamics MCQ Drill
notes:
Q1. Newton's first law of motion is also called the law of:
Answer: Inertia

Q2. The SI unit of force is:
Answer: newton (kg·m/s²)

Q3. Momentum is the product of:
Answer: mass and velocity (p = mv)

Q4. The impulse of a force equals:
Answer: the change in momentum (FΔt = Δp)

Q5. Action and reaction forces always act on:
Answer: two different bodies

Q6. The coefficient of kinetic friction is generally ______ the coefficient of static friction.
Answer: less than

Q7. The force of friction between two surfaces is directly proportional to:
Answer: the normal reaction

Q8. A gun fires a bullet; the backwards force on the gun is explained by:
Answer: conservation of linear momentum

Q9. The torque of a force about a point is zero when the force acts:
Answer: along the line through the pivot (perpendicular distance d = 0)

Q10. The angle of repose on a plane is related to friction by:
Answer: tanθ = μ

class-11/physics/unit-4-dynamics/sets/02.title: Practice Set 2 — Dynamics Short Questions
notes:
Q1. State Newton's three laws of motion.
Answer: 1st — inertia (no net force ⇒ no change in velocity); 2nd — F = ma/dp·dt; 3rd — equal and opposite action–reaction on different bodies.

Q2. Show that action and reaction forces do not cancel each other.
Answer: They act on different bodies, so no single body has both forces; net force on each body is separate (F = ma applies to one body's forces).

Q3. Define impulse and prove the impulse–momentum theorem.
Answer: Impulse J = FΔt; from F = ma and a = (v − u)/t, FΔt = m(v − u) = mv − mu = Δp.

Q4. Why do footballers pull their hands back while catching a fast ball?
Answer: Extending the stopping time Δt reduces the average force F = Δp/Δt (change of momentum is fixed), so the catch is less painful.

Q5. State the laws of solid friction and describe one way to verify them.
Answer: f ∝ N (with μ the constant), independent of area of contact; verified by pulling a block with a spring balance on a horizontal surface — friction rises to a limiting value then drops as sliding begins.

Q6. A rocket moves forward even in empty space. Explain.
Answer: It ejects gas backwards; by conservation of momentum the rocket gains equal forward momentum — no external medium needed.

Q7. Define torque and write the conditions of equilibrium of a rigid body.
Answer: Torque τ = F·d (perpendicular distance to pivot). Equilibrium: ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0.

class-11e/biology/faunal-diversity/examp.title: Plasmodium life cycle — practice
class-11e/biology/faunal-diversity/examp.topicTitle: Paramecium caudatum, Plasmodium vivax: habits and habitat, structure, reproduction, life-cycle
notes: **Practice 1:** Name the definitive host and the intermediate host of Plasmodium vivax. **Answer:** Definitive host — female Anopheles mosquito (sexual cycle, sporogony); intermediate host — human (asexual cycle, schizogony).

**Practice 2:** Which stage of Plasmodium is transmitted to humans by the mosquito, and how? **Answer:** The sporozoite. It is injected into the blood with mosquito saliva when an infected female Anopheles bites.

**Practice 3:** Why does the fever of tertian malaria recur after 48 hours? **Answer:** The RBC cycle of P. vivax is synchronised to ~48 h — every cycle, the RBCs burst together and release merozoites + haemozoin into the plasma, causing the fever paroxysm.

**Practice 4 — Order the stages.** Put in sequence: oocyst – sporozoite – gametocyte – zygote – ookinete – merozoite. **Answer:** gametocyte → zygote → ookinete → oocyst → sporozoite; separately (liver/blood): sporozoite → … → merozoite.

**Practice 5 — True/False:** (a) Plasmodium falciparum causes the most dangerous (malignant) form of malaria — TRUE; (b) The zygote develops inside liver cells of the human. **FALSE, it forms inside the mosquito stomach wall (ookinete → oocyst); the human liver holds sporozoites → schizonts → micromerozoites.)**

**Practice 6 — Short note: 'Exo-erythrocytic cycle.'** **Answer:** The second liver cycle: cryptomerozoites enter fresh liver cells and become metacryptomerozoites; large ones repeat the liver cycle, small ones invade RBCs to begin the erythrocytic cycle. P. vivax also forms dormant hypnozoites here (cause of relapse).
